No. 62, to readjust the representation in
the House of Commons, resumed			from

Rt. Hon. R. L	. BORDEN:	Mr. Speaker, when the	debate	was	adjourned two days	ago,	we	hadunder consideration	whether	the	committee should consist of seven members, as in	1903, or whether it shouldconsist	of nine	members, as suggested by my hon. friends opposite. I adhere to the view I expressed before, that seven is a better number than nine. It seems to me, notwithstanding all that has been said'by my hon. friends, that the reasons for increasing the number from seven to nine are more fanciful than substantial. The object of establishing the committee was, that a certain number of gentlemen on each side of the House should be able to meet and put forward, in respect of all questions that might arise before that committee, the views entertained on one side or the other and safeguard the interests of the country from their several standpoints. Therefore, so far as my own individual opinion is concerned, I cannot say that I have been very much impressed by the considerations which have been urged for the increase in the number of the committee. However, it is a matter upon which there might be a legitimate divergence of opinion, although, in my judgment, the smaller the number forming a committee such as this the more probability there is that it will accomplish satisfactory and effective work. My hon. friends on the other side are desirous of increasing the number beyond that which was agreed upon by both sides of the House in 1903, and, although they seem to attach to it what I consider undue importance, I am not disposed to be unreasonable on the subject. Therefore, when I come to move that the Bill be referred, I shall move that it be referred to a committee of nine and not to a committee of seven.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I appreciate
the courtesy of my right hon. friend
in assenting to our views that the committee should be composed of nine instead of seven members. I agree in principle with my right hon. friend that large committees are not desirable, and, as a rule, I think more work is effected by a small committee-by one of five or even of three-than by a large one. But this is a very special matter, and, apart from the main work of the committee, that is to say, setting down the principles upon which the redistribution is to be made, there must be a large proportion of technical work to be done in the mapping out of constituencies in the several provinces. I have asked my right hon. friend to agree to a committee of nine, so that the different groups of the population might be represented-the Maritime provinces, Quebec, Ontario and the Western provinces. The ninth member will be the umpire, and if he succeeds in reconciling the differences that may arise, he will be worthy of all honour.
Motion agreed to.

I shall make a very brief statement as to the construction and the work of the commission. The resolution out of which the commission grew was passed in the Imperial Conference in 1911-I am not going back further than that to inquire into the genesis of the commission. In pursuance of that unanimous resolution, a Royal Commission was appointed consisting jf eleven members, six being appointed by the British Government and one by each of the overseas dominions. The members of that commission at the present time, although death and other circumstances have caused a few changes, are: For Great Britain, Sir Edgar Vinpent, who represents particularly the financial side; Sir H. Rider Haggard, who is a poet and farmer and represents very largely the rural interests, which are not unpoetical by any means; Mr. Tatlow, who represents the railroad interests in a special way; Mr. Lorimer
92S

of Glasgow, who represents the great industrial interests particularly in the line of iron and steel and machinery made therefrom, and Mr. Garnett, who represents the large cotton manufacturing industries of the central part of England. For South Africa, Sir Richard Solomon was the trade commissioner who worked with us at the two earlier sessions, but unfortunately for the commission, and for South Africa, he succumbed to a sudden illness and passed away. In his place, when I left England, no one had yet been appointed; but, as the commission is at present in South Africa or very close to it, there is little doubt but that a South African member has been added to the commission. Australia was represented from the first by Mr. Donald Campbell, who is prominent in public life, and who adds to his general all-round knowledge the fact of having been a labour member and identified closely- with labour interests in the Commonwealth of Australia. Newfoundland is represented by Mr. Edgar R. Bowring. The Dominion of New Zealand is represented by Mr. I. .R. Sinclair, a member of the Upper House. I myself have the onus of conducting the work so far as Canada is concerned. At the conference of 1911 it was pretty strongly represented by some members of that conference that Cabinet ministers or men of Cabinet rank should he appointed to that commission, and I think Mr. Fisher's idea was to carry that out. Possibly the great separating distance between Australia and the mother country militated somewhat against that idea, taken in connection with the fact that the elections were pretty nearly due in Australia, .and that since the appointment of the commission there has been a somewhat spectacular and arduous political contest in that country.
It is sometimes a matter of criticism that a member of a government should take a position of this kind, -and the objection is plausible that he should have enough work to do in his own department without being absent in other countries for a somewhat long period. The criticism may go for what it is worth. I am extremely glad that I have had the privilege of being upon that commission, and that during the later period of a somewhat long political life I have been enabled to (realize what I have always had an ambition to accomplish-a wide, and to as large an extent as possible, intimate acquaintance with the British Empire in all its important distributed

parts. I have tried not to neglect my department, whilst at the same time giving my attention to the work of that commission. If further years of public service are allowed me in Canada, I am quite sure that the knowledge I have obtained and the widening of my views in connection with my work in this respect may not be without some advantage to the work of my public life and to the work of Parliament as well.
The commission was organized in the 3arly part of 1912, and during a portion of the year took evidence in London. Then the summer holidays intervened, and two months of the autumn were taken up in a second session of the commission in London. The commission works in two ways. First, it works through the medium of collected statistics, for the furnishing of which it relies on the dominions themselves. All the treasures of statistical information which bear upon the general subject matter of the commission's investigation are requisitioned from the dominions and from the Government of the United Kingdom. These statistics are collected and tabulated, and, as luminously as possible, used to illustrate the objects aimed at in the pursuit of information, and, ultimately, are considered in the recommendations made by the commission. That is a very large and important part of the commission's work. The second part, however, is none the less important. One of the most important features of this part of its work is the opportunity that is given to the commission to take in what you may call the atmosphere of the different dominions and of the United Kingdom itself. Sitting at your desk in your office, you may have all the statistics of all the portions of the British Empire piled about you, and, though you .may go through them with the utmost diligence, they are dry bones compared with what they become after you have travelled through and inquired into, and, as it were, taken on a portion of the active thought and life, commercial and otherwise, of the countries whose statistics you are studying. This living and vital atmosphere which the commission takes in during its travels tffough the different dominions, forms	the most
important part of its investigations, and will give, I	am	sure,	a determining tendency to the recommendations which the commission may	ultimately
make. In addition to that, and, in fact, to make that more effective, sittings are held consecutively in the important centres,

where men who are experts in the different areas of information which are to be explored -by the commission are, in good time beforehand, notified to prepare and have ready to submit, in answer to questions or as a memorandum, their knowledge, which is put into print and goes into the hands of the commissioners before they visit that country. So that all these important memorandums and answers to questions by officials, and by experts in various lines, are placed in the hands of the commissioners and studied by them. From that study and knowledge there comes the third process of their work, which is the actual bringing out and making clear, by questions upon abstruse or not well-understood points, the [DOT]information suggested by the memoranda and briefs and answers to questions which -have been tabulated as I have stated, and put in the hands of the commissioners. That will furnish the committee with an idea of what goes on, but that is not all. Travelling as they do, the commissioners, of course, have access to the -best sources of information, and are continually in communication with men from whom they glean knowledge which could not otherwise be obtained. To all that they add the final touch of visiting personally and looking into the different activities, industries and productivities, (if there be such a word), which form the basis of their inquisition. In all these ways, therefore, it will be seen that men who are intelligent and capable and fairly well up in their different lines have an unexampled opportunity of becoming acquainted intimately with the resources, the capabilities, the possibilities and the currents of trade of the countries visited, -and of furnishing themselves with such information as will enable them to make recommendations by which and through which all these matters may be better developed, better coordinated and all worked together for the common imperial uplift and development.
After having, not finished, but mostly carried out their investigations in Great Britain, the commission last year visited Australia and New Zealand. They visited every state of the Commonwealth and all parts of the Dominion of New Zealand and carried out their work as I have detailed. The evidence taken in Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand has now been printed, and the first interim report, which is simply a covering report, and the second interim Teport, which deals particularly with special subjects in Australia and New 59
Zealand, have been printed and presented to the Imperial Government. As quickly as possible these will be furnished to members of this House, and distributed as widely as is reasonable throughout the country as a whole.
One advantage that Canada will have in the matter is that all this evidence and the interim report will be placed in the hands of those who are to prepare their briefs and answers to questions in Canada. They will therefore have the benefit, if they choose to use it-and it is a somewhat arduous task to use it fully-of all the evidence, and the opinions that have been gained in the preceding part of the travels of the commission.
On the 7th of this month the commission left England for South Africa. Returning from South Africa, after a short interval, they will, during the present year, make a tour of Newfoundland and Canada, beginning in Newfoundland somewhere about the latter part of the month of July, and from there make their way through every province to the coast. That itinerary is now being considered and laid out. The length of time which will be given by that commission to Newfoundland and Canada will be about three months. I think I have now given a resume of the constitution and the general work of the commission. I shall be glad to answer any questions.

The committee have no doubt listened with very great interest to the explanations which have been given by my hon. friend of the work of this Imperial Commission. The graphic and even feeling way in which he has presented his observations, is certainly an evidence, if evidence were needed, of the very great importance he attaches to it. I agree with him, that this commission can be of the greatest possible importance; and I have no doubt that in view of the able men who compose it, the final report must be of great service and must link together, commercially at first and otherwise also, the British Empire. Trade, after all, is perhaps the greatest bond of union to-day amongst civilized nations and if, a3 a result of this commission, there is developed within the British Empire a greater amount of trade and a greater appreciation of it, the work of the commission will be amply justified.
I have taken exception to my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) being a member of this commission. I 'stated so in a casual way when he was absent and I have to repeat it in



his presence. No one would question the ability of my hon. friend to serve as a member; no one even discusses his qualifications in that respect. But, Sir, the very argument that my hon. friend has given in favour of his presence on that commission is the best argument in support of my contention that he should not be a member of that commission. He has stated that he attaches great importance to and has been able to realize a long-cherished wish in being able to
4 p.m. become acquainted personally with all portions of the British Empire. My hon. friend has visited Australia and New Zealand, but this commission will sit in a few days in South Africa and my hon. friend will not have the advantage of being present in South Africa, so that he might know the advantages of South Africa and the manner in which trade could be developed with that country. My hon. friend has his parliamentary duties to perform and those parliamentary duties keep him here in Ottawa while the commission is sitting in South Africa. This is the only exception I take to the presence of my friend on that commission. When we were in office we had made a recommendation to the Imperial Government as to the Canadian representation, but when my hon. friends came into office this recommendation was cancelled. I do not wish to go into that part of the i3ubject to-day. The Government thought that they should be represented on the commission by a man of their own political creed and for this there may be some justification. This office was, to a certain extent, not devoid of political considerations, and, therefore, if the Government wished to have a man of their own faith as a member of that commission I do not question this decision and I shall pass it by now. But I have to repeat to my hon. friend that whilst I do not hesitate to say that he is as well able as any man in this country to perform the work of that commission, I cannot help regretting that at the present time he cannot do his work on the commission because his duties as a minister of the Crown keep him here in Ottawa. That fact alone is a justification of the criticism I have ventured to offer, that he should not have accepted a post on that commission. Do I understand that my hon. friend has placed an interim report of the commission on the table of the House?
Yes, I placed the report, and the evidence, on the table of the House.
I sent for it to the office, but they told me it was not there.

I shall see that my right hon. friend gets a complete copy. I might say that I have about seventy copies, but these are not sufficient for distribution to each member of the House. It is intended to use these copies for distribution to those who are to be contributors of papers and so on. I have sent five copies to the Parliamentary Library. As soon as we get other copies, the members will be looked after.
Will the report be printed here?

All of this matter is set up and printed in London. They are pretty bulky volumes, and it is just a question whether we shall obtain them there, if we can get them at about the cost of printing and paper, or set up the type ourselves, which, I think, would be very much more expensive. I am now communicating with the Colonial Office to know whether we can get our supply from them at first hand.
Who will act for Canada on the commission in South Africa?

It seldom happens that all the members of the commission are present in any one of the dominions. For instance, last year in Australia and in New Zealand, South Africa was not represented. But I shall promise my right hon. friend that. as I get, from week to week, the evidence taken in South Africa, I shall read it carefully and possibly not lose too much. I may not get that peculiar atmosphere I spoke of, but I shall get all the rest. Now I think my right hon. friend is a little bit to blame for my not going to South Africa. I understood that he expressed a great desire to have me present in the House this year, and so I cut out South Africa.
I am always glad to have my hon. friend here, and that was partly the reason for my request. But I not only wanted him for my own satisfaction; I wanted him to do his duty.
Might I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if this commission is seized of the question of ocean freight rates?

I will venture to make a short statement with reference to that. During the recess the Government took

up "the question-it was pressed upon them from many sources-of heightened freight rates, and discrimination in freight rates as between different grades of articles between Canada and the United Kingdom; and in the end Mr. Drayton, chairman of the Railway Commission, was sent over to confer with the British authorities and with the shipping companies. The prominent question at that time was as to the control of freight rates on the ocean. We had gone, as everybody knows, to a very large expense to facilitate transport through the different districts of the country, and from ocean to ocean, and we constituted a board which had the ultimate controlling power over rates to be charged on that whole inland system of transport. When, however, goods leave our country, or come into our country from over seas, they traverse the ocean where we have no control outside of our own limit, and where it is impossible for any one country to exercise control. One idea that underlay the sending over of Mr. Drayton was to confer with the British Government as to what might be done towards establishing a joint control over freight rates between the United Kingdom and Canada. Mr. Drayton took up the subject there with his usual ability. He had a great deal of knowledge when he left home, and gleaned a great deal more when he was in England. He conferred with the Board of Trade, the Colonial Office and other permanent bodies. The idea was to have a joint commission appointed by the United Kingdom and Canada to take the whole matter into consideration, and for them to make an investigation and then recommend some measure for the control of ocean freight rates. The British Government did not favour the special commission for some reasons, one of which- and it was a reason which appealed with force to the Canadian Government-was that no such commission could be effected without getting first the sanction of their parliament, which would take time. The Royal Commission was already sitting and it had powers wide enough to take up that subject. In Australia, New Zealand, and partially in Great Britain, it had already taken evidence with reference to ocean freight rates, discriminations, bills of lading and such like, and the British Government proposed that this matter should be turned over to the Dominions Royal Commission and that they should make the investigation. Canada agreed to that, and the' matter was placed in the hands of the commission. The commission has 59*
taken the initial steps for an investigation in Great Britain. They will also carry on a somewhat cognate investigation in South Africa, where this complaint is also rife; and when the commission comes to Canada next year a fuli opportunity will be given to the interested parties to state their case and give their evidence before that commission. That, I think, is a short answer to the question of my hon. friend from South York.

I cannot quite
endorse that way of dealing with a matter of such vital importance to the people of this country. This ocean combine is operative to-day. The increase of ocean freight rates is the greatest tax that has been placed on the Canadian farmer. The mode of dealing with it outlined by the Minister of Trade and Commerce will take a great deal of time. From the deliberative way a British commission goes about its work, five or even ten years is a reasonable period for them to take, in hearing evidence and making a report. This is a matter that affects the welfare of our whole Canadian west and interests the whole country, and we are now told that that question which so vitally affects Canada is to be dealt with by a Royal Commission and out of the jurisdiction of this House. I do not believe in the Parliament of Canada abdicating a function that belongs to it and handing it over to a Royal Commission. The hon. gentleman in his lucid explanation said: We have a railway commission in this country but it has not jurisdiction over ocean freight rates. I dissent entirely from that statement. I say we have jurisdiction over ocean freight rates, both in our Railway Commission and in this Parliament, and in other ways, and I maintain that a cure of this grievance can be immediately effected. I can imagine it to be possible, if we are to uphold that doctrine, that there will be no cure in the matter of this ocean combine for several years. I believe that our Railway Commission has jurisdiction over freight from its origination in the West, and its transport through Canada and across the ocean, to the place where it is landed; at least we have jurisdiction over the people who are handling our commerce and who have put this unjust tax on the faimers of this country. And to show how unjust it is, I wish to say that a commission -a quick-acting commission-was appointed by the Government of Saskatchewan to investigate what it cost the western farmer to raise his grain and other products, what it cost to market it, and what profit there

was in it for himself. A report of that investigation was presented the other day, the outstanding features of which report were, first, that there had been an immense increase in the freights paid for river and lake transportation to the seaboard, and, secondly, there had been 100 per cent increase in ocean freight rates; so that, as I gather, this unjust combine on our lakes and on the Atlantic has taken almost ten cents a bushel from the net receipts of the western farmer for his wheat. The hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce, has established a very good law in connection with a special board of our own for the inspection of wheat and other grains, its storage and the way in which it is shipped. This .board has more or less jurisdiction over the products of the West. It has been a first-class law.
This Parliament is committed to an enormous expenditure for ports, canals, and ocean terminals and we are giving great subsidies to railways in order to give the Canadian farmer the cheapest possible transportation for his products to the consuming market. But the more we appear to do and the more money we spend, the higher are the charges that are put upon the farmer. Whatever may be the saving, here at home and by our own efforts, somebody is going to take it all away from us or from the farmer, and put it in his own pocket. That is being done by this Atlantic combine. The head of the Atlantic combine is the Canadian Pacific railway, the Canadian Northern railway, the Grand Trunk railway, and the Inland Lake and River combine that has been formed. These people are all within our jurisdiction, and every one of them is constantly coming to us for favours, for legislation of one kind and another, and yet we do not propose to deal with them. We do not even deal with them through the Railway Commission, which, I say, is seized of jurisdiction. We do not propose to deal with them when they come here and ask for favours. For instance, we gave a great favour to the Canadian Pacific railway the other day when we granted them rights over the Intercolonial railway, and we are giving other railways favours over our railways as well as the use of the ports that we are building. The improvement of the St. Lawrence, the lighthouse service, everything that we do for the benefit of the farmers of Canada in order to better the price they may get for their products, is all being made nugatory by the action of the ocean combine, composed of people who are within our jurisdiction.

It is not good national policy to turn this question over to an Imperial Commission which is seized of a great many other things, which is not likely to be able, by reason of the many other matters engaging its attention, to get to the bottom of this question and to make a report which will be satisfactory, and which will be subject to co-operative legislation in the various portions of the empire. If there is a reference to that commission I see no remedy for the people of the West in regard to this ocean combine, for the next ten years. Yet we are going ahead and spending money hand over fist in developing our transportation facilities, while at the same time allowing the railway companies and steamship companies that we have created, to have the advantage of all these things and to take all the cream by means of this unjust ocean combine. Is that good policy? Is it a fair thing to tell the people of Canada that there is to be no relief now from these unjust charges ? Again I say that the increased charges on ocean traffic represent one hundred per cent above what they were three years ago. There is talk of a dispute between some of the larger companies not doing business with Canada in regard to passenger service. They are having a row over that, but they do not row over the transportation of grain, apparently. They are all in-I will not say as thick as thieves-but they are all as close as they can be together to uphold these ex-horbitant rates. And they are exhorbitant. Any carrier that in one year doubles its rate by means of a combine, is doing an unjust and an unlawful thing, and those who do it, in my mind, are outlaws.
Before this House I arraign these men for conspiring against the people of Canada, and I say it is up to the Parliament and Government of Canada to have no more negotiations, or to grant no more favours to any of these people who are parties to this unjust combine. The people of the West are asking-perhaps they are always asking; perhaps it is the nature of the animal always to be asking for something -but the people of the West are asking for improved transportation, and we are doing our best apparently to give it to them. But we shut our eyes to those who take advantage of everything, and instead of the advantage going to the farmer it goes to the transportation company.
Not only is there this ocean combine, but the worst combine that was ever formed in connection with transportation is the inland combine in the lakes, canal and river navigation. The same people are in

it. Every vessel that is owned in Canada, and doing business on the Great Lakes, is in that combine. They made a great flotation of bonds the other day to carry it out. Yet we say that we are unable to reach them. They have put up their freight rates. To show how close the combine is right at the present time, I have been informed, and I believe it is true, that the rate from Port Arthur to the sea is exactly the same by boat as it is by rail. Formerly the great check we had on the railways was the competition of navigation. Now that has ceased. Not many years ago I put to an old member of this House, now dead, the question: Who holds up the canal enlargement in Canada? He said: Don't you know? It is the railways. It is a fact that for twenty-five or thirty years the improvement of canal and river navigation was held back by the railways within our own border. They were persistently opposed to inland navigation, but now that we are going ahead and propose to have canals capable of passing through even ocean steamships, what good will it be if the steamships and the inland boats are in the hands and under the control of a combine that controls the ocean and our inland waters and which also controls our railways? It is three in one; it is a trinity and it is a most unfair trinity and one that it will require the greatest courage and the highest policy, and a policy of immediate action, to grapple with. The railways would not want a better proposition than that this question should be held up for several years before a royal commission.
The same question is up in the United States, and they are now passing legislation to deal with it. They have appointed commissions to disassociate the railways from navigation propositions, and they are gradually working out the problem. Who is it that has been holding back the construction of' the Panama canal?
The United States railways tried to get control of all the steamship lines through the Panama canal, and this unholy alliance has been found out and is being dissolved. The United States Government are taking precautions to ensure that the canal will be absolutely free to all nations; they are taking action against this alliance, and they are doing so by means of legislation within the United States. My contention is that we can do the same in Canada. Let us not abandon the jurisdiction that this House, this Government and our Railway Commission have in connection with this matter. Jurisdiction is
not altogether a matter of law; it is also a matter of policy, especially when these corporations are coming as suitors for favours at every session of Parliament. We have jurisdiction both by law and by policy that ought to be able to bring these corporations to time. I hope and trust that the question will not go to the Dominions Commission, but even if it should, that does not exonerate this Parliament or the Government or our Railway Commission from trying to effect an immediate cure of that substantial grievance.
We are spending millions of money; we have created at an enormous cost a commission that was to give relief to the people, but now we confess that we are not ourselves able to remedy grievances. We are told we have to go across the ocean to enlist the co-operation of England, of South Africa, of Australia, and of the rest of the British dominions. It is not good policy; it is not national policy; it is not parliamentary policy for this Parliament to abandon its jurisdiction or to plead that we are unable to deal with a grievance inflicted on us by a creature of our own, in the shape of a corporation. We cannot afford to make any such confession of inability before these corporations that we have within our own bounds. If they over-ride Parliament in this, what next will they attempt to do? They fight us at every turn; they antagonize our own national railway; they do not wish to see us [DOT]establish parcel post. If we now confess that they are not within our jurisdiction, why make all this fuss and feather about trying to improve transportation in this country? We might as well throw the money into the sea if we do not retain jurisdiction over these corporations, and if we do not keep absolute control of the rates on freight, not only through our own country, but until it reaches its destination.
I think some hon. gentleman in this House made the statement that, rather than pay $35,000,000 for dreadnoughts, we ought to put that sum into a state-owned ocean steamship line. I would sooner put $35,000,000, or whatever the sum was, into a Canadian owned ocean steamship line than wait for this Dominion Commission to find out the facts or to confess that we have no jurisdiction over the greatest grievance that we have in Canada to-day.
I appeal to the members from the West that they have a substantial grievance to-day, and that it is no answer to that

grievance to say that it must go to an imperial commission. I am for Canada first, every time; I am for national policy every time, and I am for the jurisdiction of Canada over every citizen, and. over every creature she has created in the way of corporations.
Hear, hear.

I am glad my right
hon. friend endorses that idea. I think that national policy will also be endorsed on this side of the House and by every Canadian. I brought this question up in another form the other day, and I intend to bring it up whenever the opportunity arises. The opportunity is here to-day. The people are watching what Parliament is doing. Something has been done, but as fast as we improve the situation, along come these creatures of ours and they claim everything, and defy us, and leave the farmers of this country without a reasonable profit.
Just one word more. We want to settle the Canadian West. We are inviting immigrants from the United States and from all over the world to settle in that country. We have built all the railways in the West and we are building all these interior and terminal elevators. We have subsidized steamship lines; we are building harbours; we have the Intercolonial railway as a regulator of railway rates, and we intend to have it extended in a proper manner. Yet doing all these things, we are not able to give the farmers of Canada a single advantage in the way of transportation. We shall not succeed in building up this West if we have to wait for five or ten years to abolish this ocean combine. It must be cured now or the people will not go to the West. I ask the hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House to study what the profits of the Canadian farmer are on the wheat he is raising in the West, and they will find they are almost nil.

The profit is very
small indeed.

Yes, they 'say that the cost was, if I remember well, 62 cents, and the market 67 cents. I do not quite agree with that, yet I know that these men gave the most careful consideration to it. The commission went abroad, and the two things that they ran up against were the combine on the inland waters and the combine on the ocean. But are we to tell the 
people of the West that they have to wait all this time to cure that grievance? If so, I say, it will give a black eye to the Canadian west, and I do not want to see that, But greater than that is the question whether we are to abandon our rights and the jurisdiction we have over the corporations that we create and say, ' non possumus.' Think of it! After forty-five years of the establishment of this Confederation, after combining half the North American continent into one for the purpose of progress and good government, we are supposed to confess to-day that the control of freight charges on the main products of the country has passed out of our hands and that we must go outside our country to seek for redress. I cannot accept that doctrine.

May I ask the hon. gentleman, what would be his concrete remedy for the situation? Would he have Parliament hold up the steamship and railway subsidies until these companies agree to a satisfactory rate?

I am a great believer
in ' Putting in the probe,' a3 they say in the United States. The question that came up here to-day is that we have no organization for investigation under federal law. The right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) told me, when he was the head of the Government, to go to Mr. Foy for the enforcement of federal laws.

I will not
tell the hon. gentleman to go to Mr. Foy in relation to ocean combines.

No, but I brought up the question of the enforcement of Dominion laws and showed that we have no machinery for the sufficient enforcement of those laws. On a former occasion when I brought this matter up, the present Prime Minister admitted the strength of my argument. If we had to-day an Attorney General whose duty it was to enforce the federal laws- and I am not casting any reflections on the present occupant of that position, but am criticising the condition of the law-if we had an attorney general authorized to put in the probe and to employ the necessary officers for that purpose, and if we had the machinery which the Americans have in their Grand Jury system, then we could send for these people and have them explain the facts. We could send for Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, put him in the box, and ask him to explain to us this ocean freight rate combine. The people of Canada would be

wise in one day to the condition of affairs, and this Parliament could find a way to meet the difficulty. I am not going to give the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) the exact details of how I would proceed against these people; but I would convince them that they were in the hands of Parliament and that we intended to find a way to meet any difficulties that arose. For instance, for every cent which they added to the freight rate on the ocean, we could take off one cent of the freight rates on land, and for every cent the inland navigation companies overcharged-and it is not pretended that they are not within our jurisdiction-I would regulate them; and I would not go to England, or Australia, or South Africa to find a remedy, but I would find that remedy here. First of all we need to have an Attorney General backed by legislation which will be really effective. Oh! it is absurd to say that we in Canada, after forty-six years of Confederation have not the machinery for the enforcing of our own law. I have pointed out to this House, time and time again, what is the significant feature of every important Bill passed by the Congress of the United States. It is a provision that the enforcement of any law rests with the Attorney General of the United States and his sub-attorneys, and that so many thousands or hundreds of thousands of dollars are appropriated annually for the enforcement of the law. I say there is a cure for this ocean freight rate combine, and it is not to be found by going to England; it is right here, through our own Attorney General or Solicitor General. Here would be a fine opportunity for the young Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) to distinguish himself with the people of the West. Give him power to send for Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, for the representative of the Allan Steamship Company-a contractor with the Government for the transport of mails, and owned, I believe, by the Canadian Pacific railway -to send for Sir William Mackenzie-and he was in town yesterday; we could have served notice on him to come before this officer of the Government-and the representative of the Grand Trunk Steamship line, whoever he may be. Let us have before us these men whose ships tie up at our docks. If the Kaiser had this matter in hand, do you suppose he would let any one tie up at a dock in Germany who was an outlaw or an unfair dealer with the people of Germany? He not only would not give them a contract for the transport
of the German mails, but he would not even let them tie up to the dock; nor should we. We have every one of these sinners within our jurisdiction, we can administer proper punishment, and we can get immediate relief, if we undertake to do it, and do it within Parliament. But we cannot obtain it by a roundabout way. I am talking on this line especially to impress my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) with the idea that what he proposes to do before that very busy commission will not succeed, but that if Parliament will this session pass a law giving jurisdiction over this matter and will appoint an official with the powers of an inquisitor-and the hon. gentleman himself spoke of inquisitions that they were to have under this commission-
I was not speaking historically.	[DOT]

' Inquisitions ' is a very good word, and I use it not in the historical but in the dictionary sense, to wit, investigation. If we should this session pass a little Act empowering our Solicitor General to send for these offenders against the law in the way of transportation, and, as they say in the States, put in the probe, the evil would cease the next day or, if publicity did not do it, we could find another way. I think it is up to the Government to revise its policy in regard to this ocean rate combine and to proceed immediately, directly, and by all means within our jurisdiction, to break that combine, to expose the men who are in it, and to show that they are a Canadian organization, and within our law; and to compel them to do justice, or else confession. And, I do not want to confess-I will never confess-that there is not a cure within the Canadian Parliament for every grievance of this kind that exists in Canada.

I am afraid that if we continue the discussion on this line we might cover the field of the world's affairs and not get our items through. I do not rise to object to what my hon. friend has said, for I always listen with a great deal of pleasure to him. In a way, he is an outlaw himself, and he exemplifies his doctrine by his practice. However, while I do not intend to discuss this question which has been raised in the House by my hon. friend, I want to take just a moment or two to allay some of his fears.
In the first place, I do not believe that the

Surely this is the proper
time to discuss the matter which has been brought to our attention by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean). I think the minister should be gratified at the manner in which the hon. gentleman has brought this very important matter to our notice, because it is a matter in which the people of this country are surely very deeply interested. It is alarming that the history of transportation in Canada during the past few years gives indisputable evidence of the fact that the more we improve our transportation facilities the more advantage is taken o.f these improvements, not by the people but by the transportation companies themselves. While the price ol wheat may go down, the freight charges on the wheat we export from this country constantly increase. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has, during the past twelve months, in his tour of certain parts of the world, undertaken the very commendable object of promoting the interests of the trade and commerce of this country. While the hon. minister has been trying to find new markets for Canadian produce, our transportation companies have been so increasing the charges on the produce we have to export that any good the minister may have accomplished or attempted to accomplish has been nullified. The hon. member for South York said something about the West always wanting things. Perhaps that is the nature of the animal; if so, it is a commendable nature. I may tell the hon. member -for South York that the western people are a progressive people; they are not satisfied to let well enough alone. They want to keep on doing better all the time, and they certainly are not satisfied with present conditions so far as the export of their surplus produce is concerned. They are not content with the fact that the charges made for the transportation of thelir produce by the inland and ocean navigation companies have been increasing during the last few years, although the price of wheat has been going down. This Government has, I was almost going to say, penalized the farmers of the West;

perhaps that is too strong a term. At least they have adjudged that the farmers of the West may not sell their surplus wheat in the nearest market, just across the line; they must send it to Liverpool, and other foreign markets. I trust that one of the results of the minister's visit to China will be the shipping of Canadian wheat eastward as well as westward,
As a result of the position taken by this Government, we are compelled to use these means of transportation in getting our wheat to the markets of the world; and we are confronted by this situation, that year b>
year the freight rates are increasing. We may deepen the Welland canal, as the hon. member for South York said, we may undertake great expenditures, if v/e please, for the improvement of our transportation facilities, but no matter what we may do, under present conditions, we are not benefiting the producers of Canada by these expenditures.
What is the increase in the last five years?

About fifty to one hundred per cent in inland navigation, and in ocean navigation, I believe, more. The grievance calls for a remedy, and we are asked by the minister to be patient and wait for the report of this commission, which will decide as to who has jurisdiction and by what method the solution of this difficulty may be arrived at. I must say that I agree entirely with the hon. member for South York that this House should not have the patience to wait for the report of a commission which may be indefinite or may be conclusive, but which in the end may devise no way by which we can arrive at a satisfactory settlement of the problem. It is quite true that the bulk of the inland navigation companies that do business in Canada, as well as the lines that carry our exports to the old country, are controlled by the railway companies of this country. We surely have jurisdiction over the railway companies, and we can and should have jurisdiction over the inland navigation companies; and by indirect, if not by direct means, we can surely exercise some influence over the ocean steamship lines. I was going to ask the hon. member for South York if he does not think there are one or two very useful indirect ways by which the rates of the ocean steamship lines could be lessened. It is my recollection that in 1897, when the British preference was established, that it had a very marked effect
on ocean freight rates, the reason being that the ships carrying our exports to the old country had a return cargo owing to the increased trade between Canada and the mother country. As I understand, it is the great object of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to promote trade between the component parts of the British Empire. How better could we increase this commerce between the mother country and Canada and the other parts of the empire than by increasing the British preference so that the ocean going ships that carry our produce to the British markets and the other parts of the British Empire, would have the privilege of bringing back a full cargo instead of half a cargo. That surely would have an important effect in lessening ocean freight rates. As to the question of jurisdiction, the hon. member for South York did not arrive at a definite conclusion as to how we could devise a remedy. I do not think we ought to be asked to wait until this Imperial Commission gave us an answer to the question. I think that this House has within its confines enough legal ability and talent to take this question -into consideration and devise ways and means by which it can be settled. I wonder if the hon. member for South York would not think it advisable to propose to the Government and to the House that a special committee of this House be appointed to deal with this question, to sift out, to discover the ways and means by which Canada, through legislation, can have jurisdiction not only over our inland shipping companies but over the ocean lines as well, in so far as those lines do business with Canadian ports. I give that suggestion to the hon. member for South York.
That is better than going to England.

I give that suggestion, confident that in the personnel of the Government, including that new member of the Government to whom the hon. member for South York has referred, the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), there is sufficient ability to solve the problem. We read some months ago in the newspapers that the Solicitor General proposed to deal with this very question of ocean freight rates. I do not know how he is dealing with it, but I think that he and other members of the Government and of this House might very well be appointed a special committee to give this question their consideration and to devise ways and means to bring about

legislation by which we shall have jurisdiction over this question of inland and ocean navigation tariffs. I appreciate the position taken by the hon. member for South York on this question. He certainly is speaking in the interests of the farmers of the West, and I would assure the hon. member for South York that in the days to come-and they are not very far away, I trust-when there is a change of Government in this country, if his remarks are not taken as seriously as they should be by the present Government, I personally would very strongly endorse the view that no man in this House would be better fitted to take charge of that department, the Attorney General's Department, which would deal with this question, than the hon. member for South York.

I am quite prepared to support this vote for the Imperial Trade Commission, and am quite prepared to believe everything that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said in regard to its value. While it is unfortunate that the hon. gentleman cannot be in this House and in South Africa at the same time, we are glad to have his presence and assistance here. That, however, is not to be understood as endorsing the idea that because we have an Imperial Trade Commission,-no doubt composed of good men and having large powers and authority, and a commission which will do good work,-we should not pay attention to the problems which are pressing upon us most closely and most seriously, and which can be attended to, in a measure or altogether, without calling in the services of that commission. If the vote for the Imperial trade commission is to be given as a reason why we should not give every attention that lie3 in our power to the problems that are pressing upon us, immediate and direct, I would be strongly in favour of striking the vote out. It is the problems that are pressing most closely that require our attention rather than those which are at a distance. We are glad to have the distant problems attended to in due course, but not at the sacrifice of attention to the problems close at hand. To show how pressing the problem of trade and transportation is, let me take the liberty of bringing to the attentioii of the House the matured conclusion of a commission of inquiry appointed by the Saskatchewan Government. The commission was composed of practical men of that province, who travelled in Europe where they were given every opportunity to acquire information.

Only a preliminary report has so far been issued, but it contains matters of such vital importance to this country that I desire to bring it to the attention of the House. All matters in this country, whether trade, finance or any other thing, finally come down to the question of the production of wheat and the price of wheat, and the conclusion of that commission 13 that while the cost of wheat production has increased by 12'15 per cent since the year 1909, the cost of marketing the wheat has increased by about 15 per cent. That is to say, while it costs the farmer 12-15 per cent more to produce his wheat, it costs him 15 per cent more to market it than it did in 1909.

And the price
has also gone down?

Yes. The Liverpool quotations fell from $1.23 in 1907 to 98 cents per bushel in 1913: a difference of 25 cents a bushel on the market price, a difference of 12-15 per cent in production and a difference of 15 per cent in the cost of marketing. The figures are arrived at by making a calculation on the handling of a thousand bushel carload. To quote the report:
The services enumerated are those performed in connection with 1,000 bushels of No. 3 Northern wheat shipped through a country elevator in Saskatchewan, hauled to Winnipeg, there sampled and graded by the Government, sold on commission to an exporter, hauled to Fort William, unloaded, weighed, received in store, cleaned and insured at a terminal elevator, inspected out into a lake steamer before the close of navigation, carried to a Georgian hay or lake Erie port, unloaded through a transfer elevator into a railway car, hauled to Montreal, unloaded from the car into a transfer elevator, loaded thence into a steamer and carried to Liverpool or London. This procedure and route are selected because more grain has been handled by this procedure than by any other and more has been exported via this route than by any other Canadian route.
The charges may be grouped naturally under two heads:
1.	Charges (paid directly by grower and shipper of consigned grain.
2.	Charges paid directly by purchaser of consigned grain, but indirectly by grower and shipper because deducted from the price the grain realized.
I will not trouble the House with the details but the conclusion is, that in 1909 it cost $304.60 to market a carload of wheat from the province of Saskatchewan, and in 1913 it cost $346.60.
Might I ask whether that additional charge is entirely attributable to additional freight rates?

I was just going to give the details of the increases. It is not necessary for me to give the whole details. All the charges remain the same in 1909 and 1913, except those I will mention: the rates of interest has increased; the estimated increase in interest on 1,000 bushel carload valued at $700, is $2; the increase in lake carrying charges is from $10 in 1909 to $20 in 1913. That is just double. The ocean steamship charges have been
5 p.m. increased from $40 per 1,000 bushels to $75. Those are the only increases. The increase in hank interest is trifling but it may be counted. But the increase in cost of lake transportation is serious; it has been doubled and the cost of ocean transportation has been almost doubled, and this cost, as the report points out, necessarily is deducted from the price the producer receives.
What was the lake rate per bushel last fall and in 1909?

This report does not take into account last year's rates. The summary contains only a general computation but I happen to have the figures on lake rates, and my information is that in the season of 1913 the lake rates varied from If to 3| cents a bushel.
Is that with storage?

I could not say. This responsible commission appointed by the Saskatchewan Government has declared that the cost of lake transportation doubled since 1909 and that, in conjunction with the increase of ocean freight rates and the increased cost of production, and in connection with the drop in the world's prices, has produced what may be considered as a crisis in wheat production in the western country and is a matter of such great importance as to call for every attention that can be given to it by this Parliament and the Government to relieve the conditions in whole or in part. While dealing with this question of lake freights, let me give the House some information that I am sure will interest the people of Eastern Canada as well as those of Western Canada. Of the grain that went forward from Canadian ports at the head of the lakes from August, 1913, to the close of navigation in December, 75,000,000 bushels went by United States ports as against 58,000,000 bushels by Canadian ports.
Is that mixed grain or wheat alone?

That is all grain. That is something that should make those members who are interested directly or indirectly in the shipping ports of Eastern Canada recognize that they too have an interest in this question of the transportation of western grain. When Canada does not handle, through her own ocean ports, half of the grain that she produces, it is certainly an indication that there is something radically wrong in connection with transportation.
Is there any difference between the freight rates on the Great Lakes going by an American port, such as Buffalo, and the rates through a Canadian port?

My hon. friend can hardly ask that question because unless there was a difference the grain would not go that way. It must be of advantage to ship by way of Buffalo or the grain would not go by way of Buffalo.

In this report of the commission the statement is made that the grain of Canada, to reach the market in Liverpool, pays more than the grain of any qther country in the world. That would cover the case of the United States, and the rate is lower in the United States.

The condition, as it appears to my mind, is this: on account of the shipping combine on the Great Lakes, which is a Canadian combine and which controls the rates between Port Arthur and Midland, it has been necessary for shippers to take advantage of American vessels available for that trade, which vessels could not carry from Port Arthur to Midland, and, therefore, these shippers, in order to get the lower rate on their grain, had to ship by an American bottom through an American port. As a matter of fact, that is precisely what occurred during the past season. The freight rate during the past season averaged lower than it did the season before because a larger proportion of Canadian grain went by American bottoms through American ports. That is why the grain has to go that way, and that is what brought the rate down.
Will the hon. gentleman give us any exact figures and not mere assumption as to the Canadian rates on the Great Lakes as compared with the American rates via Buffalo?
The rates are invariably the same.

Naturally the rates remain on a par because, when the American boats carrying grain to Buffalo come into the competition, if the Canadian boats carrying [DOT]to Midland did not carry at the same rate the grain would -all go to Buffalo. That is elementary. The question of interest to this House is not what the rates are but the question of interest, so far as the western producer is concerned, is that the rates are higher than they used to be and higher than they ought to be. To the eastern representative, who is concerned with eastern Canadian shipping points, the question of interest is that the freight is going to American ports. Whatever the reason may be, Canada is losing that trade. If the transportation companies are losing trade business interests in every way are losing trade, and I say it is for the Government to wake up to this situation and, instead of awaiting the report of an imperial trade commission, deal with this matter that is immediately in hand. This is a matter which ought to be under the control of this Government. My hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) desires me to read to the House a statement from the Saskatchewan report which is as follows:
It costs the farmers more to have the exportable surplus of Western Canada's grain crop placed on present ultimate market than the farmers of any other large exporting country have to pay.
That is a startling statement and when it is taken in conjunction with the increased cost of production and the drop in prices in the world's markets, it is notice of a situation in this country that must have very far reaching effects. It has such a direct bearing on the present condition of the country that I think the country should wake up and realize what the position of affairs really is. Our farmers are producing their grain at a loss and not at a profit. Our country is not getting the benefit of the transportation of grain in such proportion as it should. One reason in large measure is the combine of the lake vessels which has driven Canadian grain to American ports.
Do the farmers in the Northwest pay more per bushel per mile than do the farmers in any other country?

My hon. friend asks me a question that I cannot answer, and that I could not be expected to answer. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, with all the resources that he has at his command, could not answer that question. It does 
not matter what other people pay; the question is, what do we pay and can we afford to pay it? That is the essential question, and if the answer is, as the Saskatchewan Grain Commission has answered, that we are not getting for our grain a price at which we can afford to produce it, then certainly there must be a change of the methods of marketing and transport, or our products must be restricted in proportion. Everybody knows that the restriction in any degree of western products is bound to have a serious, nay a disastrous effect upon the welfare of this whole Dominion. Unless production in the West can be moderately and reasonably increased from year to year for many years, there will be serious loss and injury throughout the rest of Canada, because our industrial establishments, our commercial organizations, our financial institutions have all been organized and capitalized with a view to meeting the increase of production that is expected.

This is very interesting and important, but I would gather this inference from the report of the commission, and also from the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver), that there is a combine on the lakes so far as Canadian vessels are concerned, and that there is no combine so far as American vessels going to Buffalo are concerned. I also draw the inference that, so far as Canadian bottoms that carry the grain over to the old country axe concerned, there is a combine, and so far as American bottoms are concerned there is not a combine. Are these the facts in connection with the matter? The statement that it costs more to carry our. western grain to market than grain grown in any other part of the world does not sound very well, and requires investigation. The only country that you could compare with western Canada would be the western states. So far as the Argentine republic or any of ther other wheat-growing countries are concerned, the traffic is by sea, and ocean freight rates are of course less than railway rates. If my inference is correct that there is a combine in Canada and not in the United States, then I think the matter can be very easily explained. I would like to know if my hon. friend can give any information on these two points.

On the lakes there is a
combine amongst Canadian shipping interests. There is not a combine amongst American shipping interests. The latter

enter into our trade only when their trade is slack. We did not get their competition in the season of 1912 to the same extent that we did in the season of 1913, because they were busier at home in 1912 than in 1913 It was because the ore carrying trade fell off in 1913 that the American vessels came into our trade and thereby reduced the rates for 1913 as compared with the rates for 1912. In order that the western farmer shall get the benefit of that competition, the eastern port interests must lose. That is an undesirable condition.

The proof that
American wheat is carried to market at a lower rate than Canadian wheat lies in the fact, that if there were free wheat in this country to-day, the bulk of our wheat would go to market through the United States and not through Canada, unless the Canadian railways came down to American rates. So far as I can see the only people who today are opposing free wheat, are the railways, because, if they can keep the wheat from going into the United States, they can reap a bigger profit on their "freight rates.

The American rates
are not lower.

The American freight
rates are lower.
What are they?

I am taking it on the general proposition which I .put before the House the other day that the opposition to free wheat comes from the Canadian railways, because they are enjoying higher rates to-day. If we had free wheat, our wheat would go through the United States unless the Canadian railways reduced their rates, and they would have to do so.
Tell us what the rates are.
The rates are lower in the United 'States than they are in Canada.
Anybody could say that.
I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver); I will give the details later on. My conviction is that the opposition to free wheat is because it entails the reduction of Canadian rates.

So far as my part of the country is concerned, the rate from Boissevain to Fort William and the rate from Rolla, a town directly south of us and a few miles across the border, to Duluth, are exactly the same.

I am not questioning that at all. I am pointing out a condition that exists beyond any question. There is no possible doubt that the eastern Canadian ports lost the transportation of a large pro portion of that 75,000,000 bushels of grain because of the Canadian shipping combine on the upper lakes.
What cure does the hon. member suggest?

I am trying to arouse the interest and attention of the House and measurably of the country to a condition as it exists. Unless that interest can be aroused, there is no use proposing a remedy. Unless the country believes that it is being hurt and hurt in this particular, there is no remedy required. I wish to put it beyond argument that there is a damaging condition; that it is seriously damaging. If I can impress that upon the House and the country, then I shall be glad to go into any discussion as to a remedy for it.
The point is that there is on the upper lakes a combine of Canadian shipping interests which is detrimental to the western producer and also to the interests of eastern ocean shipping ports.
I am not antagonistic to the views that the hon. gentleman is putting forward. He has my entire sympathy in regard to this question. All I desire is a little more light upon the subject.
Let us have a committee.

I hope the force with
which I have made my statement is not construed by my hon. friend as offering any objection to his question or to any discussion that may arise. I speak strongly because I feel strongly; because I feel that the condition is serious and that the House should be thoroughly aware of how serious it is.
My hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaff-ner) asks as to the conditions on the ocean. As I understand, the great lines which run to Canadian and American ports are in the one combine. The combine is the same to New York as it is to Montreal, so far as the combine is concerned; but there is this difference, that the tramp steamers which are not in the combine have access to United States ports on terms of less insurance that they have in Canadian ports. Shippers from American ports have that advantage over us, because of that that condition.

Now, in regard to the ocean rates. Every man has receive ,i within the past day or two the report of the Council of the Quebec Board of Trade for 1913, in which there is information which seems to me to be almost startling; so far, at any rate as the principle involved is concerned. The assertion is made that the Allan Line carries certain classes of freight, mentioned here, for less money to Montreal than to Quebec, and that as a matter of fact, freight is systematically carried to Montreal by steamer and shipped back to Quebec by rail. Here are some of the figures:	Oilcloth in rolls to Montreal 25s.; ito Quebec 27s. and 6d. Woollen goods in bales, to Montreal 25s., to Quebec 35s. Pease in bags to Montreal 20s., to Quebec 22s. and 6d.

How about
whisky?

I had just reached that item, and I am sure my hon. friend will be interested. Whisky in cases to Montreal 30s., to Quebeo 32s. 6d.; liquor in cases, to Montreal 30s.; to Quebeo, 32s. 6d. It is quite evident that there is discrimination by ocean steamships as between Canadian ports. We have got quite used to the condition on the railways under which it is as cheap or cheaper-or used to be cheaper, I am not sure but that it is yet- to ship oats from Edmonton destined to Kamloops first to Vancouver and thence to Kamloops rather than direct. It is news, however, that the same conditions prevail in regard to ocean traffic and that the city of Quebeo, at tide water about 180 miles nearer Liverpool than Montreal, pays 2s. 6d. per 100 lbs., or whatever it may be, more than Montreal pays for freight landed there. I do not know whether an Imperial Trade Commission is necessary to deal with that question; I do not know whether it is a question that is considered to be of serious interest-it is certainly far removed from the locality in which I have any direct interest. But I draw attention to it to let the House know that discrimination and high charges are not peculiar to the West, but that the other parts of Canada suffer somewhat similar conditions.
The main point, however, is that so far as wheat production is concerned, there is work for the Government of Canada to do and work for this Parliament to do, in dealing with the conditions which I have shown on the authority of the Saskatchewan Commission to be so serious, not only to western Canada, but to Canada as a whole. These conditions demand immediate attention; not

waiting for the report of an Imperial Trade Commission-which may be altogether useful in itself. These conditions press close home; they ought to be, if they are not, under the jurisdiction of Parliament; and they ought to be dealt with now by Parliament and by the Government

I understood the hon. gentleman to say that the cost to the farmer of wheat-producing land had increased very much and that its producing qualities had decreased very much. Could the hon. gentleman tell us why the land has increased in price while its producing qualities have decreased?
I think the hon. gentleman misunderstood me; for I did not say the quality of the land had decreased, but the returns from production to the farmer had decreased.
I understood that among the causes of increased cost was the increase in the price of the land.
Yes.

If the wheat is so much
cheaper and so much more expensive to produce, the producing value of the land is >so much less?
No doubt.
Why, then, is there an increase in the price while the producing qualities are decreasing?

For several years the
price of wheat was increasing, and while it was on the increase and before the cost of production had risen owing to the increased cost of articles that the farmer had to buy, land naturally increased in value. But under the conditions that now exist land is not increasing in value and cannot increase in value when the financial returns from the working of that land are on the decrease. The land itself must decrease in value, and that itself is a serious condition. We need not say too much about it, but we all must realize that it is inevitably the case and that it is to the last degree serious to every interest in this country.

My hon. friend has declared that it is time that this Government and this Parliament should ' wake up.' These are two very good words. I suppose they have been applicable at other times als well as at the present. An interesting side-light-a bit of

history which ought not to escape attention entirely-is thrown upon this discussion to-day by some documents which are at hand and from which I am going to quote to a very small extent. My hon. friend was a member of a very powerful government in this country at a time when the freight rates were going up, moving skyward, rocketing. My hon. friend was from the West then, as he is now; he had the interest of the West at heart, as he has now; the complaints poured into his ears, as he says they are pouring into his ears now. What was done by him and his Government at that time? I am not deterred in the least by the two Latin words ' tu quoque' which will be trotted out in a little time. I am bringing the matter up by way of a little historical sidelight on the position of my hon. friend.

If the hon. gentleman
wants the answer, I can give it to him in a moment, and I will not use the tu quoque either.

The hon. gentleman may give an answer hut the record speaks plainly, and though he is fairly accurate sometimes the record is a little more accurate than his assertion. So, I propose to take the record. In the early part of 1910, protests showered in upon the then Government with reference to the enhancement of ocean freight rates. The Minister of Railways took the matter up with Judge Mabee who at that time was Chairman of the Railway Board. Judge Mabee prepared what I would call an able memorandum-and he was considered to be an able lawyer. I am not going to read all that memorandum, but I wish to refer to two or three parts of it. In the first place-he states-and that contravenes the dictum of my learned friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) on the law -that the jurisdiction of these controlling bodies his own included-
-Is limited to the land or land and inland water movement. In other words the moment that an export traffic reaches the seaboard of any of those three countries, Government control over it is absolutely lost.
He discusses the matter further by saying:
Under the present law, when these shipments reach Montreal, control over the rates and conditions of transportation is lost, the result being that for two-thirds of the total distance the traffic moves at the rates the ocean carriers choose to make.
He proceeds to say:
The time to obtain control over the rates upon this traffic is while it is comparatively in its infancy and not after enormous development has taken place and shipping trusts of all kinds have grown up.
He concludes by suggesting that an international tribunal consisting of the English Railway and Canal Traffic Commission and the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, or certain defined members of those commissions, could by joint legislation be empowered to control all these matters.
What is the date of that memorandum?

February 12, 1910. The
Minister of External Affairs at that time (Mr. Murphy) presented that report to Council, and a minute of Council was passed, pressing upon the Colonial Secretary the desirability of having a joint tribunal appointed to regulate and control ocean freights. On February 28 Earl Grey sent a copy of that Order in Council, which was dated February 26, 1910, with a covering despatch, to Lord Crewe, who communicated it to the Board of Trade on March 31. The Board of Trade took it into consideration, and on August 4 it advised Lord Crewe, in effect, that a joint inquiry be made by persons designated by the British and Canadian Governments. On August 18 Lord Crewe transmitted that communication to the Canadian Government, asking the Governor General to be kind enough to transmit, as soon as possible, any further observations that might be made by the Canadian Ministry. On August 31, Mr. Walker, a clerk in the office of External Affairs, brought this despatch to the attention of the Minister of Railways. There the matter rested until November 30, 1910, when a despatch was received from Mr. Harcourt, Secretary of State for the Colonies, asking for the minister's views at an early date. Nothing resulted, and on December 20, Mr. Pope called the attention of the Department of Railways to Mr. Harcourt's despatch. From that time on there was no response, and on March 14 the Governor General's office communicated with Mr. Pope, saying that a further despatch had been received from Mr Harcourt, dated March 14, asking again for a reply to his former despatch. All these things took place, and yet there was no action by the Minister of Railways or by the Government in power at that time. Notwithstanding the fact that in February,

1910, hon. gentlemen opposite committed themselves to the principle of a joint tribunal to investigate and control, particulars concerning which were in the hands of the Secretary of State for the Colonies by August of that year, and a communication from him, asking for further observations, received by the Canadian ministry by the last of August of the same year-and that this was followed up by three separate despatches asking for a reply to the first-nothing was done, hon. gentlemen who now, through the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) tell this Government, in tones of thunder, to wake up, at that time did absolutely nothing; nor did they do anything before they went out of office. The criticism is made that this is a matter of such importance that time is an element. If this matter had been put into the hands of a joint tribunal for inquiry and for recommendation, with the disposition of the British Government favourable and accordant action on the part of the Government oi Canada, there might have been to-day a joint control of ocean freight rates between Canada and the old country. But my hon. friends did nothing, and now, two years afterwards, they come to us with that trumpet note:	'Wake up; time is very
precious/ I just wish to put this matter on the records of the House to show what a most important lapse of memory has taken place and to show that hon. gentlemen opposite for twelve long months had not the time to reply to a despatch from the Secretary of State for the Colonies. Under that joint tribunal and commission there might have been an actual and substantial lowering of last year's and this year's freight rates by control of ocean transit, to the benefit of the farmers of the West, about whom these gentlemen, and rightly so, are so much concerned. When the western farmers listen to these fervid appeals for action now, in February, 1914, let them remember, and apportion their judgment accordingly, that in 1910 there was a method offered by which the Government of that day might have had control over the ocean rates upon all grains carried from the West to Great Britain during this last year and the year preceding if they had simply taken the trouble to answer a despatch and put into operation an effective control of these rates.

My right hon. friend is
not quite right in that. I said I was not deterred by any assertion of the tu quoque argument from bringing this matter before the House. It is an absolute tu quoque argument, but it is an historical fact.

Certainly, and my hon. friend has had the advantage which I have not had of perusing the correspondence. He stated he had only read some partial extracts from it to the House. I do not know what are the parts he has left out. I do not know if there is anything involved which had better be put before the House, and I invite him, since he has put part of the correspondence before the House, to put it all on the table so that we may have the advantage of looking at it.
Certainly.

In the meantime I have only to say: what is the use of having a change of government? What is the use of all the inflammatory speeches we had at one time if these gentlemen, on coming into office, are to do just as their predecessors did? Suppose we were lax in 1910 and 1911, is that any justification why my hon. friends, coming after us, should be lax in 1911, 1912, 1913 and 1914. My right hon. friend found that correspondence in the Archives of the Government. He stated that the British Government awaited our reply. Why did he not send a reply? Has he made any reply since the 21st of September 1911? Not a word. By his own confession he has not. And all he has to say now is: You have been derelict in this matter but we have not been any more derelict than you have been. Was it for this that he was put in office?
