We have had no excuse for this laches of the Government except: You have done as we have done. That is not what the people expect. The people are commencing to be disappointed, and they have good reason to be disappointed. They expected when a new government was in office that everything that was wrong with the late Government would be better. But by the confession of my hon. friend himself we left that matter in 1910 for him to deal with; he comes in, a new broom-and the new broom does not

sweep at all. I would remind him that in 1911 we were very busy.
Too busy to look after the farmers.
Not too busy to look after the farmers, we were looking after the farmers at that time.
Looking after their votes.

And the
farmers have told my hon. friend again and again: Give us the United States market for our wheat. That is the best way of dealing with the freight rates question. My hon. friend will not even communicate with the English Government, and when the farmers come here asking to have a competitive rate, my hon. friend turns a deaf ear to them. That is all the explanation my hon. friend has to give. Can he say that we were at all negligent ? In the midst of a stormy session in 1911 when I had to leave the business of the session to attend the Imperial Conference, in England, this very question came up, and it was I who moved at the Imperial Conference for the establishment of that very Imperial Commission for which my hon. friend is now asking an appropriation. To this commission I myself moved that this very matter of ocean freight rates should be referred; and yet my hon. friend has the audacity to say we were derelict in our duty in respect to it.
Just a word to clear up some of the mists that are around the mind of my right hon. friend.
Better look to yourself. '

No doubt my right hon. friend is perfectly right in saying that they were looking after the farmers in 1911; that is, they were looking after the farmers' votes. They were awfully diligent about that, but they did not show the same diligence in looking after the farmers' freight rates for nine, ten or twelve months before. It was a tremendous task, no doubt, it required much time for consideration. But what were the facts of the case ? In February, 1910, they had come to the conclusion that a joint tribunal was the proper thing, and had asked the British Government if they would join with them in constituting one. They had made up their minds, there was no necessity for any time to consider, they had come to a conclusion on a point of policy and their policy was a joint tribunal, if it could be brought 60
about, between Great Britain and ourselves, in order to control freight rates. In August, 1910, the British Government acceded to their matured opinions and the way was cleared, all obstacles to the appointment of the tribunal were swept away, except one, and that was the time that was necessary for some minister of the Government to sit down and write a despatch agreeing to have a joint tribunal between Canada and Great Britain, and naming the persons who should act for Canada. For 12 whole months no reply was sent to an acceptance of a proposal which they had made. But my right hon. friend is a little out again. He said the new broom did not sweep, meaning the present Government. Neither did theirs. But the facts are the very opposite. They made the handle of the broom; the British Government made the brush of the broom, they had the handle fitted so that one-half minute's work would have put it into the brush so that the brush would sweep; but they were so anxious for the farmers' votes that they did not want to sweep in order that the farmers freight rates might be reduced. We came into office, and to-day not only is there a proposal, but there is an accepted arrangement, by which a joint tribunal is to-day looking into this very matter of control of ocean freight rates. So that our broom has swept, and we have shown that we are looking after the farmers' interests, having got their votes. My right hon. friend looked after them, but he did not get all of them. We got our proper proportion of them and addressed ourselves gratefully to guard the farmers in that respect.
At six o'clock, the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock Mr. W. F. MACLEAN: I want to refer to some of the incidents of the debate this afternoon. I appreciate very much what my good friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce said about my being a lawyer and an outlaw. That term may be rather a compliment in this country. But it is a strange thing that any one who criticises in a reasonable way-and I think I was reasonable enough-the railways or other corporations in this country, should be called a corporation baiter, and be told that he is most unfair and does not know what he is talking about. A friend of mine in the Cabinet also spoke of me the other day as John the Baptist, because I happened to have some



original views as to public affairs in this country.
That is a compliment.

I think it is a compliment. I am proud that I am not a lawyer, and I can say to the hon. gentleman who was Minister of Marine that perhaps he is a sea lawyer. We all know that a sea lawyer is a man who has an opinion of his own. In a very delicate way, he suggested to the Chairman this afternoon that perhaps I was an outlaw as regards the discussion I raised, although I imagine I was quite within the rules of the House. Be that as it may, I want to recall to him and to other members of the House a little incident which occurred in this House touching on my legal knowledge and which also bears on this question. A good many years ago, I was trying to call the attention of the House to an amendment that I proposed to the Railway Act, that express rates should be controlled by the Railway Commission, and the present eminent and learned Chief Justice of Canada who was then the Minister of Justice, got up in the House and gave his high legal opinion that I was unconstitutional, inasmuch as express rates concerned inland navigation, stages and railways, which were outside the jurisdiction of this House. He was backed up in that opinion by another eminent lawyer in the House, now the Prime Minister, and between the two the House was persuaded that I was acting unconstitutionally and my proposal was turned down. But, it was not long before this House adopted the principle that we had control over express rates and we made the express companies come to time. In the same way I say we have control over these steamboat companies. They load at our ports and we can get at them in that way. Furthermore, we subsidize them to carry His Majesty's mails. We build ports for them, and they are part of the railroads of this country. These railroad companies give bills of lading from the point of origination of the freight rates across to the other side, and in that way they come within our jurisdiction. We have jurisdiction over them in a great many other ways. I know that the usual way of getting by any question is to get a lawyer's opinion on it. They presented the opinion of the late Chairman of the Railway Commission who suggested that a commission go across the ocean, and the Government of that day took advantage of that. And now the same thing has happened to-day, only in a more veiled and 
expert way. Another commission is to go and look at conditions in the Old Country. That will not do. You can always take advantage of a legal subterfuge of that kind. I contend that this Parliament has full jurisdiction over these companies, and that we do not need to go to England for any assistance in that matter. All the facts could be elicited by a parliamentary committee of this House. We could send for all these people and find out how this eombine originated, and who are the members of it, and let the people of Canada know.. If we did that, we should find out that all these companies are the creatures of this Parliament, and are within the jurisdiction of Parliament; and if we made the issue as between them and the people of Canada it would have such an effect on them that that combine would be dissolved the very next day. But if we are to put off dealing with this matter until some commission reports on it, and until other countries have to be consulted, the evils will never be cured. My suggestion is, and I make it with all respect, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce take this question with him to the Imperial Commission and let him take with him all the information that can be obtained by a parliamentary committee of this House. I do not know whether that Commission has the power to summon and swear witnesses and get evidence as we have here. We could bring them all here within a couple of days and get all the facts about this ocean combine, what its object is, under what law they are organized, and why they seek to take away from the Canadian farmer every advantage that accrues to him because of the immense expenditure this country has made for the improvement of navigation. If we are going to spend, not a hundred million dollars but two or three hundred million dollars, on new ports, on deepening canals, and on the improvement of navigation generally, and a shipping combine is to be allowed to take away all this from us, then we had better confess that this is not a self-governing country, that we are not competent to deal with these questions and that the Parliament of Canada is less than the corporations it has created. This is a most serious question and it has to be settled. It cannot be trifled with, as it was trifled with by the previous Government according to the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon, and it will be more or less trifled with if we send it to the commission. A parliamentary committee could get all the facts in a very

short time, and then if we found we could not deal with it we could give those facts to the minister; but I am confident that an investigating committee of this House could get the facts and force a dissolution of that combine within a month, or two at the most.

When the Minister of
Trade and Commerce was speaking, he dealt with the condition that I had endeavoured to lay before the House and the country in regard to the grain trade of Canada. I cannot put into words how strongly I feel that the country must be disappointed at not hearing from the hon. gentleman, either a denial of the conditions or a suggested remedy for them. The hon. gentleman satisfied himself in dealing with a condition that must be admitted to be of the gravest national character, by calling in question the inaction of his predecessors in office. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the questions before Canada at the present time in regard to the price of wheat, in regard to the condition of transportation, in regard to the consequences to the trade, finances and industry of Canada at large, is not ameliorated, or remedied by any reference to the conduct or misconduct of my hon. friend's predecessors in office. I do not think it would be a useful expenditure of time to defend the position of the late Government in this matter that my hon, friend has seen fit to attack. He asserts that the late Government opened the question of ocean freight rates with the Imperial Government and carrried the matter no further. I am not in a position to give reasons for the action, or inaction, of that day, nor, do I think it is material to the discussion.
Let me draw my hon. friend's attention to the fact that there is a serious change in conditions between that date and the present, and that the change of conditions emphasizes to such a degree the necessity of action by the present Government that no possible measure of shortcomings by the late Government relieves them from the responsibility. Since the late Government went out of office the price to the farmer for his product has decreased by 8 cents a bushel according to the report of the Saskatchewan Grain Commission. Assuming the marketable product of the wheat of the West to be 150,000,000 bushels, my hon. friend can see by these figures that the difference in value to the farmer for his product as between this year and the year in which my hon. friend took office is a matter of some 60i
$12,000,000. That surely is a sum of sufficient amount to show that if it was a matter of urgency then it is a matter of still more pressing urgency to-day. If the late Government may have been justified we will say, in putting something else before the question of ocean freight rates, these are 12,000,000 reasons why the present Government are not so justified in taking no other action.
It is not only the fact that the price to the farmer has been reduced by reason of the shipping combine, as well as by the operations of the world's markets, but it is also a fact that the cost of production has been increased. The reports that are published from month to month by the Department of Labour give a statement as to the increased cost of living throughout Canada. That increased cost of living affects the farmer on the prairie just as it affects everybody else throughout the country, and that makes it as necessary that he should receive a greater price for his product if he is to get an equal profit upon it as that the salaried official in the city of Ottawa should receive an increase in his salary if he is going to be in as good a financial position at the end of this year as last year. Not only is there an increase in the cost of living, but there has been an increase in the bank rate of interest. The increase in the cost of land has to be provided for and, according to the report of the Saskatchewan Commission, the farmer is to-day twelve per cent worse off in the cost of production than he was in 1909. The greater part of the increase in the cost of production has taken place in the latter two years rather than in the former two years. My hon. friend must therefore admit that if the position was urgent in 1910 it is proportionately more urgent to-day.
But instead of my hon. friend coming forward with a remedy, he comes forward with the statement that the late Government failed to take action in regard to a matter as to which .they themselves had raised the question. If that is the only answer that my hon. friend has to give, if all the country has to look for at the hands of this Government is the reply, that whatever the conditions may have been in the past history of Canada no action dealing with that condition was taken and if that is a justification for no action being taken at the present moment, all I have to say is that the condition of the country is not hopeful under the administration of my hon. friend.
The condition that exists calls for

remedy, but I want to point out that I was not putting forward the responsibility of the Government in regard to ocean freight rates. I was careful not to put that responsibility forward because I appreciate very fully that with the best of intentions this Government, or any Government, must, in the nature of things, have such a limited measure of control over ocean freight rates that there can be no great results looked for with any degree of certainty from effort in that regard. We will be glad if the efforts that are put forward by the present Government result favourably in securing a reduction. We will be glad to give them every credit for their success, if success they achieve. But I cannot look with any great hope upon the prospect. A joint arrangement between the authorities of Canada and the authorities of Great Britain in regard to shipping rates across the ocean must strike anybody as a rather one-sided proposition. While Canada sends and receives a large part of the freight, the vessels are owned in Great Britain, and the dividends are paid in Great Britain. It stands to reason that British interests, looking at those interests as humanly selfish, naturally they would look for the greatest revenue that could be secured from the operations of the ships. Therefore, in the nature of things, so far as assistance from the British end of the conference is concerned, we can at best expect sympathetic consideration of the conditions under which we labour. I shall be glad if I am disappointed. I shall be pleased if the Government is able to do better than I hope, but I must say that I do not consider the outlook at all hopeful in that regard. It was for that reason, as well as for others, that I urged upon the Government attention to those matters that were within their control and under their responsibility. I protested against setting up the idea of looking for relief across the ocean, where relief might never be secured, and of ignoring the responsibility of providing such measure of relief as could be secured nearer home. In regard to the shipping combine on the upper lakes, there is no doubt that it is under the jurisdiction of this Parliament.

What does the
hon. member mean by a combine on the upper lakes? Does he mean that one company has control over the freight rates, or that the different companies are combined in order to keep up the freiebt rates?
 *

I think the latter position is probably the correct one. My hon. friend is aware that one company has absorbed a large portion of the lake shipping, and therefore is in a very convenient position either to compel its competitors to come to terms or to make favourable arrangements with them. We need not traverse that ground again. The fact remains that, because of the existence of a shipping combine on the upper lakes, 76,500,000 bushels of Canadian grain found an outlet through United States ports last year as against 57,900,000 bushels through Canadian ports.
Has my hon. friend the figures of last year so that he can compare relatively what passed out by each way last year and this year?

I have not the figures,
but my information is that just in proportion as the shipping combine on the upper lakes strengthened its position, in the same proportion Canadian grain was forced into American channels.
I have an impression that the fact's of the case are that, as compared with the United States, a very much larger quantity went by way of Montreal this year than last.

I have not the figures; but it will ndt be denied, that not very many years ago Montreal was bulletined throughout America as being the leading grain shipping port of the continent; that it had actually surpassed New York in its amount of wheat shipments. That is not the fact to-day. Not only is it not the fact, but Montreal is not getting even half o.f the Canadian shipments. That is absolute evidence that something is wrong. I may be mistaken in my judgment as to the cause, but there is no question as to the fact. As I have already said and urged, a certain condition being found to exist it is the business of the Government to find out what the causes are and to prescribe the remedy. I will go so far as to suggest a remedy, a drastic one it is true, but I believe an effective remedy, only to be used in case of emergency, namely, to permit the United States shippers to carry Canadian grain from one Canadian port to another. I have some 'Confidence that that would bring the shipping combine to a realization of the fact that they did not own Canada; that they did not own the farmer of the Northwest, and that it was

not their privilege to strangle him whenever they saw fit.
There is another means whereby the farmer could be given reliei. I should not use the word 'farmer'; I should not say that the farmer could be given relief, because this is not a question of the farmer only; it is a question of the business of the Dominion of Canada.
A short time ago there was moved in this House a resolution urging upon the Government the desirability of removing the duty on wheat as a means of securing the free entry of wheat into the United States. As to the advantage of that to the Canadian farmer and to the businessman who depends upon the farmer, I quote the latest price list that I find in the Grain Growers' Guide of February 11, showing that No. 1 Northern for cash was worth 87J cents in Winnipeg and 91J cents in Minneapolis. It is, however, a well known fact that Canadian grades are higher than those of the United States and that Canadian No. 2 is quite equal to American No. 1. Therefore, the comparison would be No. 2 Northern at Winnipeg, 852 cents; No. 1 Northern at Minneapolis, 911 cents, or a difference of nearly six cents a bushel. With this market of Minneapolis standing at a figure six cents higher than the market at Winnipeg, if there is an opportunity to secure access to the Minneapolis market for Canadian wheat so that the Canadian producer could get the benefit of that six cents per bushel more, there is at least a prima facie case for the Government to take such action as would give that opportunity.

If I understand my
hon. friend's argument, it is, that, because the quotations of what he calls an equal quality of wheat in Minneapolis ranges six cents a bushel higher than in Winnipeg, therefore, if there were no duty intervening between those two points, our wheat would have an increased advantage of six cents per bushel. That is the argument if there is anything in it. It may be modified a little by saying that there would be some charges midway according to the destination of the wheat. The argument is that it is the duty that causes that difference in price between Winnipeg and Minneapolis. Suppose the hon. gentleman takes two cities in the United States, perhaps not further apart, and consults the quotations, he will find time after time a difference of two cents, three cents, four cents, five cents, six cents,
sometimes as much as nine cents a bushel between the two. There is no intervening duty there, so in that case it is clearly not the duty which makes the difference in price. Does not that lead the hon. gentleman to believe that there are other factors besides the duty, and that he has not quite proved his case from the one citation he has made? This matter of trade and prices is a pretty wide, round, long, deep business.

I am quite willing to admit that there are other factors entering into the price of wheat, and I will not urge for a moment that the removal of the duty will invariably give to the Canadian producer six cents a bushel more for his wheat. But I do say that, the conditions in Minneapolis being as they are, Minneapolis being: the great milling centre of the United States, the great wheat market of the United States, and that market showing consistently a price measurably, considerably, notably higher than that of Winnipeg-that is when Winnipeg has any wheat to sell-it is evident that the removal of the duty would accrue to the benefit of the Canadian producer. It appears to me to be a clear prima facie case, and the Government is certainly not doing its duty to the country if it does not try this matter out by actual experiment.
Is there any reason to feel that Canada cannot be the great milling country of the world, with the wheat in our own country and the mills here or to be brought here? Would not that be worth while?

My hon. friend is asking a question which rather diverts me from the argument I wish to make, but as he has asked it, I would say that mills operate not only for the purpose of grinding wheat, but also for the purpose of selling flour; and you require a population in order to have a market for flour you grind. And as long as the United States has 90,000,000 of people and Canada has only 7,000,000, there is, in the nature of the case, a much laager market for flour in the United States than in Canada, and therefore the United States must be a better milling country.

Not necessarily a larger
market for Canadian wheat.

How much flour does
the United States export to the foreign mar-' kets of the world yearly?
I could not give the information offhand.
It is a large quantity.

I know they do export a great deal of flour. But I know as a matter of fact also that they are prepared to buy our wheat, for reasons that are well known. Our wheat is required by them for the purpose of mixing with their wheat of different quality; I will not say of lower quality, but it does not command an equal price. Therefore there is a standing demand in the United States for the quality of wheat that we raise, not only because of their great home milling industry, but also because of their export milling industry; and they are willing to pay a higher price for that wheat than our Canadian millers are willing or able to pay. As to the reasons for that I do not speak, but the facts are as they are. It is not for me to weary the House with details, but I put it on the lowest possible basis: there being a prima facie case, the Government is not doing its duty by the country and by the western farmer, under the present conditions of reduced prices and higher cost of production, if it does not give the farmer an opportunity to reach more buyers by opening an important market. Everything that my hon. friend has suggested here tonight was suggested and repeated in regard to the price of cattle. When we were discussing the advantages of reciprocity with the United States, we were told-just as my hon. friend has it in his mind with regard to wheat-that, since the United States exported cattle we could not find a market for our cattle in the United States, although the United States market prices were higher. Since that time the United States duty on cattle has been removed, and the consequence has been that the price of cattle to the farmers throughout Canada has increased very substantially, not only in the county which my hon.
- friend represents, but also in the county which I represent, and he knows it perfectly well.
Not feeding cattle, but young cattle and stackers.

Cattle, anyway. There is a substantial advance in the price of cattle in that part of the country since the removal of the United States duty on cattle. The United States export cattle and they export wheat; yet they buy wheat and they buy cattle, and they will give us better prices than we get to-day.
(Mr. Morphy.]	,
Will the hon. gentleman allow me another question ? Under the conditions he lays down, the United States would be sending wheat back here free ?
Sure.

They export somewhere about 100,000,000 bushels a year of soft wheat. That would open to the American farmer in the Toledo district the market
of the Canadian farmer in Ontario, and reduce his price from ten to twenty cents a bushel. Does the hon. gentleman want that P
I do not think there would be any such reduction in price.
Authorities say so.
Of course, the authorities may be correct, but I say
If that is true, would the hon. gentleman willingly submit the Ontario farmer to it ?

I am coming to that. I am going to quote the deputation of western farmers and Ontario farmers who met this Government shortly after the opening of this session with a series of resolutions, and one of the first of these resolutions was a demand that food should be made free of taxes, because they said that taxes on food were a crime against humanity. And I say that if this duty on wheat keeps up the price of flour unduly throughout this industrial and manufacturing section of Canada, it is doing a damage to the success, the prosperity and progress of Canada, and it is not doing a corresponding benefit to the man who produces the wheat.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid the discussion is wandering beyond the scope of the resolution which is on the item ' Imperial Trade Commission.' A discussion on the question of free food is rather outside the item before the Chair.
I was only answering my hon. friend.
But you were not answering, that is the trouble.

I was trying to answer. I was doing the best I could; if I could not make my hon. friend appreciate my point of view, that is my misfortune. I was showing courtesy to my hon. friend by giving him the answer I thought best to the question he asked. I did not wish to

pursue that side of the question except in reply to him.
I assume that I shall not be out of order in having offered one or two suggestions to the minister a? to improvement of trade conditions in the country by bettering prices to the farmer, I offer as well, a third. The Canadian Gazette, of London, England, has been dealing with this question of the shipping combine. That journal has given the country the benefit of its views, and, if I may, I will offer to the House a paragraph giving the conclusion at which it arrives. After pointing out the difficulties of any enforced reduction of rates on ocean vessels, the Gazette concludes:
The densely populated towns of the motherland are the true market for Canada's produce, and the ever-expanding centres of Canada are the natural markets for the British manufacturer of goods which Canada does not and will not for many years make for herself. Let Canada buy more from England rather than from the United States and other foreign land3 and the steamship facilities and lower rates will come naturally enough. The grain-growers of the Canadian west have for some years desired a gradual increase in the British preference in the Canadian tariff with a view to the ultimate establishment of freer trade, if not * free trade,' within the British Empire.
The suggestion is that a reduction of the tariff between Canada and England would, by increasing trade between the two countries, tend to reduce the cost of shipment and thereby bring about the result that is looked for-cheapening the cost of transportation of western wheat to the Liverpool market.

Would that reduced
cost of living be effected at the expense of the West, or of the East?

I was under the impression that as everybody, both West and East, eats three meals a day and wears the same kind of clothing, anything that would reduce the cost of living anywhere would reduce it everywhere.
No, it does not.

I am quite unable to
follow my hon. friend; I was under the impression that that would be the effect. The hon. minister has declined to offer any suggestions of relief for existing conditions. I have made certain suggestions which I am sure he will not accept; I am now going to make another. He refuses to take the duty off wheat, thereby giving it free access to the markets of the United States; he refuses, I presume, to reduce the duties on goods coming from Great Britain into
Canada, thereby securing cheaper facilities for trade between this country and Great Britain; I am sure he will not take measures against the shipping combine on the upper lakes. Will he, then, increase the price of the farmer's wheat by increasing the duty on wheat? If this Government believes in a national policy, a policy of high tariffs, a policy of protection of Canadian industries, now is the time for them to show their faith in that belief.

Does the hon. gentleman
think it would be to the advantage of Canada to have a higher duty on wheat?

My hon. friend need not ask me that question; I say, certainly not. But I do say this: if this Government believes what it preaches; if it believes that a high tariff will make prosperity, that a high tariff will raise prices, now is the time for them to show their faith in that belief. Let them raise the price of the farmer's wheat by increasing the duty on wheat. Mr. Chairman, I am a protectionist.
Since when?

Always. I believe in legislation. that will improve the condition of the country, and if my hon. friends, by increasing the duty on wheat, will correspondingly increase the price of wheat to the farmer, I will support them. Do hon. gentlemen believe in what they preach, or do they not? They will not reduce the duty on the wheat, because, as my hon. friend believes, it would do the farmers harm; will they, then, increase the duty on wheat and do the farmers good? This Government has been in .power two years; during those two years the price of wheat has gone consistently down and the cost of living has gone consistently up. The area of cultivation in the western provinces, because of those conditions, has been at a standstill, if it has not decreased. Homestead entries have dropped by 9,000 in two years, as the result of the policy and administration of hon. gentlemen opposite. If this policy of theirs is good, if they believe that it is good, now is the time for them to take such action as I have suggested. But my hon. friends know that their policy is a sham; they know it is a fraud; they know they cannot better the prices of the farmers' wheat by increasing the duty on wheat, and they will not take that means of remedying existing conditions.

The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) devoted a great part of his speeches this afternoon, as well

as of his remarks this evening, to trying to prove that there was a combination in connection with freight rates on the upper lakes, and that this combination had been fostered by the present Government.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I want it to be understood distinctly that in all I said this afternoon and this evening, I kept as faT away as I could from any charge against the present Government or what they had or had not done, for the purpose of urging upon them the necessity of doing something in the future.
The hon. gentleman at least encouraged the House to believe that this combination to increase prices has sprung up within the last year or two.
No.

The hon. gentleman
pointed out the fact that there has been an amalgamation of a series of upper lakes companies, with the result that the prices for the carriage of grain on the upper lakes have been increased. If my hon. friend looks them up he will find that the rates from Lake Superior ports, Duluth or Fort William, to Buffalo or other Georgian Day points, are invariably the same. The hon. gentleman said this afternoon that the rate last year varied from one to 3J cents. He forgot to tell the committee that the rate of 3i cents included not only carriage, but also the storage of the grain in the* vessel all winter, this storage as well as carriage facilities being afforded by the vessel owner. The fact that the vessel is used as a floating elevator during the winter season throws a different light upon the matter. I wish to quote from the Buffalo Board of Trade Report-and I am sorry that it runs down only to 1908-the different prices that have prevailed on the upper lakes. In 1899 the price varied from 2i to 6 cents a bushel, which is much higher than it was last year. In 1904, the price varied from 1 cent to 5 cents a bushel; in 1905, from li to 4 cents a bushel. So hon. gentlemen will see that the rates have very often been higher than they were last year. As to the restraining of competition and the fixing of rates by these companies, let us see what the facts really are. I hold in my hand a little book issued by a Cleveland firm, which shows that approximately the number of vessels that are on the Great Lakes, both United States and Canadian, is 1,300. I do not say that these are all grain carriers; some of them are not, but a very large proportion of them are. I do not think there are over 75 
or 100 Canadian grain freighters on the upper lakes; the amalgamation of last year, to which my hon. friend referred, does not operate over 40 grain freighters. If the hon. gentleman will peruse the list he will find that the bulk o.f these freighters are very small vessels; they do not commence to compare with the large freighters of the steel trust or other United States companies.
Some of the American vessels carry thirteen thousand tons, while the bulk of the Canadian freighters carry not over three thousand tons. There are upwards of eight or ten different companies on the Canadian side. I do not believe there is any collusion or arrangement between these companies to preserve rates, and for the reason that it is an utter impossibility that a hundred vessels competing	against a
thousand could control the rates. The hon. gentleman stated this afternoon that there is always the	American competition
because the American vessels can carry the grain from Port Arthur or Fort William to Buffalo. He also stated that the export trade in grain of the port of Montreal was falling off. If he had looked up the annual report of the Board of Trade of Montreal, at page 52, he would have seen that while in 1909 there were exported from Montreal 11,691,000 bushels, the next year, there were exported 21,500,000; the next year 21,000,000; the next year 25,500,000 and in 1913, 44,000,000 bushels. The port of Montreal last year did the biggest business it has ever done. The trouble is that we have not proper facilities at Montreal. Any man who h&s done business out of Montreal can tell you that the grain is delayed there, apart and aside from the question of better rates from New York to the British Empire or to Europe. But there is no question that we have not been able to get grain away from Montreal fast enough; and in these Government elevators I think a great mistake was made last year in that people were permitted to keep grain there for speculation. I am informed that vessels lay often as long as twenty days at a time unable to load, while thousands of cars were standing in the yard. We have been making advances in the past year or two in the port of Montreal, as is shown by the report that last year we exported
44.000.	000 bushels from that port. It is quite true that at Buffalo they took in
150.000.	000 bushels. Of course the bulk of that is not exported, but is manufactured into flour right in the United States. The

business of the port of Montreal has not been a matter of a few years but of many years, and no doubt when the trade of Montreal has increased proportionately for a few years more the larger proportion of the grain now going out by American ports will go down by our own route. To argue that any combination exists on the upper lakes among the sixty or seventy-five Canadian vessels, and that they can muzzle trade and fix prices, is absurd, because last year was the first year when a combination would have been possible, yet as a matter of fact the rates last year were lower than for several years. In November and December when the greatest volume of grain is pushed forward the rates were much lower than for many 9 p.m. years before, and the Tates from Duluth to Buffalo were correspondingly in proportion just what they are from Fort William to any port on the Georgian bay. The hon. gentleman should not despair as to the trade of Canada going to the United States. Let me tell him that twenty-five years ago only one million bushels of grain came into the Georgian bay and there were only two elevators, a small one at Collingwood and one at Midland. Turn up the records in the office of the Minister of Trade and Commerce for last year and it will be seen that they handled, at Collingwood over ten million bushels; at Midland over thirty million bushels; at Port McNicoll over ten million bushels and at Depot Harbour over ten million bushels, so that in twenty-five years the trade of the Georgian bay in grain has increased from one million bushels to over fifty million bushels, something that, I think, we should be very thankful for. The whole crux of the position to-day is that the Government must advance to the work of Montreal sufficient money to equip elevators there. Whether that is done by the Government direct ot through the Montreal Harbour Commission is unimportant, but the trade has increased so that more adequate elevator accommodation should be provided. In addition to that there should be more stringent rules to compel people to pass the grain through those elevators, rather than store it with these improvements the trade of the port of Montreal would be very much increased.
On the question of the ocean freight rates I believe a great wrong is being done and it is to be hoped by everybody that the rates on the ocean liners will be decreased
very materially in the next few years. How that is to be done I know not, but I think the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), the hon. member for York (Mr. Maclean) and any other hon. gentlemen who endeavour to keep this reform to the forefront are conferring a benefit not only on the West but on the whole of Canada, and I hope that these rates may be reduced very materially.
Mr. McCREA. I think that excessive freight rates, rail and ocean, not only affect the wheat trade, and the western trade, but affect the whole of Canada. They affect everything in the shipping line, and what affects trade affects everybody, t was somewhat surprised a minute ago when the hon. member from Edmonton stated that the ocean freight rate on a thousand bushels of wheat, was formerly $40 but had increased to $75 in the last few years. The original rate would be four cents a bushel and the present rate would be seven and a half cents. When you compare that with existing rates and past rates pn lumber you will conclude that the lumber dealers have a great deal more occasion to complain than the wheat dealers, although I believe the wheat dealers have sufficient ground for complaint. In 1910 the ocean rates on lumber were anything from 32 shillings to 36 shillings per standard, or about $4.50 a thousand, from Quebec or Gaspe ports to Liverpool. The rate last year on the same class of lumber was about 65 shillings a standard, or, in other words, a little over $8 a thousand feet board measure. If you get down to actual weight per hundred, a thousand feet of lumber, if at all dry, weighs less than three thousand pounds. A standard of 1,980 feet, approximately 2,000 feet or 6,000 pounds at 65 shillings or $16, which is a little over 25 cents a hundred. That is the rate that exists to-day on spruce and lumber to Liverpool, London and other points. On square timber the rate in 1910 was 52 shillings a standard, or equal to about $10.50 a thousand. If there is any class of freight that, comparing the weight with the value, ought to have a low rate it is lumber. Nothing less the freight quoted by the steamship people to-day from Portland or even from West St. John is seventeen cents a hundred pounds-equal to $10.50 a thousand feet. The first question to be considered is, does a grievance exist? I was a little surprised at the Minister of Trade and Commerce retorting: When your party was in office what did you do? That does not seem to me to be the right way of dealing

with this matter. The next question is, have the Government any power to remedy that grievance, and if they have, what are they doing towards remedying it? It is not a question of, what one government did when in power. Gentlemen opposite did not talk that way in 1911. Then they said: the Government is not doing its duty; pu't us in office >and we will conduct the affairs of this country in a businesslike way. But we are now in the third session under the new Government and nothing has been done. If the Government have not power to remedy that grievance, is there any machinery by which they could remedy it. If there is let them get busy and do it. The whole country is suffering. To give a concrete case: in 1912 a shipper with whom I am pretty well acquainted, wished to ship timber in the winter months, but during the winter months the railway company could not supply cars. When navigation opened in Montreal, the steamship company gave a through Bill of lading for the cargo but at that time there was a strike in Liverpool and it was eighty-two days from the day the timber was loaded until it was landed at Liverpool. Timber when dressed and in shipping condition is about as perishable as fruit. If it is exposed to the sun and weather it becomes suncracked and weather beaten, so that it is unsaleable when it reaches the market. This timber reached the market in that condition, was rejected by the buyer and had to be sold at cull timber prices. When he asked the shipping interests to compensate him for this loss he got no satisfaction and he could not reach them. I am not blaming anybody especially, but that is the condition that exists. I believe that the high cost of living and high wages have something to do with these heavy ocean rates, but they are,
I maintain, out of all proportion and some remedy should be found so that the shippers of this country will not suffer as they do at present.
Trade and Commerce-Census and statistics, $75,000.

What is the state of
the census at the present time; how near is it to completion?

As to the work *completed and published, there is volume 1, containing the tables of population of Canada by provinces, census districts and *sub-districts; volume 2, tables of religions, races, birth-places, citizenship, illiteracy and infirmities; and volume 3, manufactures by provinces, districts, cities, towns, 
and incorporated villages - of 1,500 and over in population, with comparative taibles. Three volumes of the census are completed and published. Eighteen bulletins have been issued dealing with manufactures, dairying industry, agriculture in the different provinces, illiteracy, ages, and infirmities. That leaves to be completed two volumes, and the tables of volume 4, comprising the natural products of the country, namely, agricultural products, mines, forests, and fisheries aie nearly all ready for the printer. Volume 5 will contain the following tables: school attendance (that is completed), dwellings and families (completed), churche-s (partly compiled), schools and colleges (partly compiled), charitable and penal institutions (partly compiled), immigration (partly compiled). Occupations and wage earners have yet to be compiled. To sum up, three volumes are completed and published, *and of two others, one is ready 'for the printer, or nearly so, and the other has a large number of its material already compiled.
When does the minister expect the work will be completed.

It is being carried forward as rapidly as possible; I do not know exactly when it will he completed, but sufficient help is being given to the officers to carry on the work of compilation just as rapidly as it can be done.

How many are there
on the staff at present?
I could not say exactly, but outside the permanent officers I think there are about 75 on the staff.

At the last redistribution a map of the western provinces showing the population of the townships was prepared with the assistance of the Census Department. It was very convenient for us in outlining new constituencies. I would like to ask if such a map is being, or will be, prepared for* the forthcoming redistribution; or, if not, would it be possible to have such a map prepared?

I will take a note of it
and make inquiries. The map would be made in the Interior Department, we furnishing the population statistics.

It is only by means of
such a map that it would be posible to get a really accurate knowledge of the population.
