Mr. Chairman, I desire to give a word of explanation with reference to the fact that in the last census the average attendance of children at the schools of New Brunswick was reported to be very low. Under the laws of the province of New Brunswick children are not allowed to attend school until they have reached the age of six. In other provinces'it seems that children at the age of five are allowed to attend school. The average attendance in New Brunswick is lower than in some of the other provinces on account of the fact that children are not allowed to attend school before they are six years of age.
Trade and Commerce-West India cables, $38,933.33.
Has there been a reduction of cable rates?

For a long time-I do not know how long, but I suppose from the inception of the cable service into the West India Islands-the rates have been very high and they formed a veritable impediment to trade between Great Britain, this continent, including Canada, and the West India Islands. There were different companies in the West India Islands. One was the Panama Company, which worked through United States territory and through the territory from Key West and along and in conjunction with some other cables through different parts of the Islands. Then later, there came a direct cable from Halifax to Bermuda, and shortly afterwards an extension was made from Bermuda to Jamaica and Turks Island. That brought about a notable reduction as far as Jamaica and Bermuda were concerned. But the West India Direct Cable Company, terminating at Jamaica, found itself up against these cable companies that went around to the other islands, and were under certain contracts and agreements with which I will not trouble the committee. Th<# result was that cables that went by the Direct Company through to Bermuda and Jamaica were not forwarded by the other companies. They refused to give them right of way except upon their own terms and at their own charges. Competition was not gained at all so far as all the West India Islands were concerned with the building of the Halifax, Bermuda and Jamaica lines. The rates were very high, higher than in any civilized countries in the world, and there has been an attempt in various ways to
reduce them. When the West India delegates were here that matter was taken up, and as hon. gentlemen know who have read, and I suppose all have read, the Minutes of the Conference, the result was that an agreement was reached by which Canada was asked to represent to the British Government the nature of things and endeavour to bring about a reduction of the rates. Canada at that time offered to share with Great Britain whatever was necessary, in addition to the subsidy paid by the West India Islands, which was all they could afford to pay, to bring about ah amelioration. When I. went to England afterwards I took up the matter with the Postmaster General and with the two companies. To make a long story short, after a year and a half or so of negotiations the Postmaster General came to an agreement by which the West India Panama Company undertook to better its service, to give right of way to all cables which went through from Halifax to Jamaica via Bermuda, and to reduce the rates in all just about one-half of the former rates. These fates are now satisfactory to the business people of Great Britain, Canada and the West Indies.

What is the rate per
word?
There are different rates to the different islands.
From Halifax to Bermuda?
The West Indies do not participate in that rebate, if any?

The West Indies do not
participate in' the rebate. The rates per word were formerly:

Halifax to Bermuda, 48 cents a word; British Guiana, $1.44 a word; Antigua, 81 cents a word; Barbados, 91 cents a word; Dominica, 77 cents a word; Grenada, 89 cents a word; Trinidad, 98 cents a word; St. Kitts, 89 cents a word; St. Croix, $1.02 a word; St. Lucia, 85 cents a word; St. Thomas, 96 cents a word; St. Vincent, 86 cents a word.
The reduction that has been made amounts to about an even half of these rates.
Could the hon. gentleman give us the present rate?

Does it take in Porto
Rico?
No. These rates are for the British West Indies and British Guiana.

Has any new
arrangement as to cable rates been made since a year ago?

About a year or more ago some reduction was made before this negotiation came to an end. This negotiation resulted in an arrangement which I think came into force not many months ago, about the first of the year if I remember rightly. According to the practice in England, the arrangement had to go before the Treasury Board and receive the assent of the Lords of the Treasury.
Mail subsidies and steamship subventions__
steam service between Canada and the West Indies or South America or both, $340,666.66.

This is the service which was put into force the latter part of last year. There was entered into with the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company a contract, the particulars of which are pretty well known to those of the committee who have followed the service. Probably my hon. friend from Halifax has some questions or remarks to make upon this, or would he rather that I should make a general statement with reference to it?
Yes, regarding the nature of the contract.

The contract has a history which was discussed last year and the year before in the committee, and was the consequence of two or three attempts to procure a satisfactory servio? between 
Canada and the West Indies. In the first place tenders were called for these services, giving an option to tenderers for a variety of itineraries, and a variety of speeds and capacities of vessels. When the tender time came to an end, it was found that no satisfactory tenders were in. The tender time was extended until the end of December, 1912, when several tenders were in with varying prices and with different conditions of speed, of size, and of capacities of vessels. At that time negotiations were taken up with the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company, and a provisional or prospective offer was made by them. In the end, however, when all these came to be considered, some were impossible; others were withdrawn and the Government decided to enter into a contract with Pickford and Black, who proposed to associate with themselves certain foreign steamship companies, or owners, and to put on a service such as was described in their offer. Messrs. Pickford and Black, after the contract had been signed by them, were not able to get that co-operation which they expected. As a consequence the whole matter seemed to be confined to two lines.
What amount was discussed at that time with Pickford and Black and their associated English companies?

That was for the sum of $200,000 per annum for a twelve day twelve knot service. However, this did not come to anything, and it appeared to me that we were reduced to one of two things. As my hon. friend knows, charters were very high at that particular time; I think the highest that they have been in the period of heightening charters. The construction of new vessels was difficult, and costly, and, besides that, required time. When the possible arrangement with Pickford and Black fell through, there were just two alternatives. One was to have recourse to a very large and influential steamship company, enter into negotiations with it and make the best arrangements possible, and the other was to go on with the old and inefficient service that we formerly had with Pickford and Black. I took up negotiations with the Royal Mail Steamship Company, and after some time received an offer from them for the service which they are now rendering. They entered upon this service in the latter part of last year. This offer was for a fortnightly service with vessels of the description given in the con-

tract, and with an average speed of eleven knots kept up at sea.
What was the Pickford and Black contract agreement as to speed?

Do I understand that at the expiration of the steamship service which is now subsidized by the West
Indies, and which I suppose are interinsular services, they will co-operate with Canada in establishing a trunk line service with inter-insular service? Is that the idea?

There are several ideas as to the kind of service that would be best. There are those who advocate a trunk line with inter-insular service. This is advocated more by the large islands than by the small ones. But there are very great difficulties as my hon. friend knows in carrying on a service of that kind so far as Canada's portion of it is concerned, both receiving and sending out, because of the difficulties and damages of transfer from the trunk line vessels to the others in ports where almost all of the work has to be done by lighterage. There are two or three ports where the dock is approached and the service is completed over the dock, but in all the rest of the West India Islands lighterage has to perform the work of transfer both ways, and these lighterages are of varying lengths from half a mile, to two or three miles long.
Do I understand that the minister hopes that some day the West Indies will contribute to the subsidy for this particular service we are now discussing?
Yes, that is the intention of the islands themselves, and the hope we both entertain.
What did Pickford and Black receive under the contract which expired two years ago?
Somewhere about $89,000 or $90,000.

I have very little
to say about the West India steamship service contract. I must say, that personally, I should have preferred if some arrangement had been possible with Pickford and Black of Halifax, in connection with this West India service. They were the originators of the steamship service between Canada and the West Indies and naturally were obliged to devote a great deal of money in developing trade with the West Indies. I have always thought that, while the service was hardly up to the requirements, still it gave to the West Indian ports and to Canada a fairly substantial service. It is true that a superior service was frequently suggested, but I think that frequently the public were un-

fair in the nature of the service they demanded.
In my opinion the trade hardly warranted such a steamship service as many of the business men of the West India Islands and of portions of Canada were demanding from time to time. I think the minister himself has undergone a change of opinion during the past year. When the West India treaty was enacted a year ago, I rather received the impression from the hon. minister that an exceedingly modern and veil-equipped steamship service would be established between the Maritime provinces and the West Indies, and that it would at least be very decidedly superior to the service carried on by Messrs. Pick-foi d and Black. As the minister said a moment ago, under the old contract Pick-ford and Black were paid about $100,000, or less, while the present contract means an expenditure of $340,666.66. Naturally the question arises whether there is a sufficient improvement in the service to justify the increased expenditure. I have no hesitation in saying that had Messrs. Pickford and Black at any time in the past been offered a subsidy of $340,000, they would have at once placed in commission steamships equally as good as those used by the Royal Mail Steamship Company in the present service. The four ships which are en-' gaged in the present service are the Cobe-quid, the Chignecto, the Caraquet, and the Chaleur. Unfortunately the Cobequid was wrecked in the bay of Fundy recently, and, I suppose, has not yet been replaced.
I presume, however, that this vessel will be replaced by one of about the same character. The Cobequid, Chignecto and Chaleur were built in 1893, and the Caraquet in 1894, so that they are comparatively old boats. It is true that in tonnage they are in excess of the boats of the old Pickford and Black service, although there is not a very great difference so far as some of them are concerned. The four boats of the Royal Mail Steamship Company averaged about 2,900 tons each. The tonnage of the steamers of the Pickford and Black Line under the old contract was considerably less, although one or two of the boats had a tonnage of over 2,000. So far as passenger accommodation is concerned, it would not appear that the present service is a very great improvement over the old one. It is true that the passenger capacity is greater, particularly for second and third-class passengers, but the difference is not very great, and it does seem to me that 
the Government is paying a very handsome subsidy indeed for the services rendered under the present contract. In my own province, particularly in the port of Halifax, the opinion prevails amongst those who understand the need of that 'service and the West India trade, that there is not a very substantial improvement in the present West India steamship service. I do not presume to put myself before the committee as one capable of judging of the merits of the steamships now in service under the contract which we are discussing, but I have been led to the opinion which I have ventured to give by reason of the opinions I have heard expressed by persons in the port of Halifax who, I think, are competent to judge of the matter. If the minister will compare the class of boats now in the service with those previously used under the Pickford and Black contract, and consider the disparity in the amounts paid to the two companies, he will see that one might naturally expect a very materially improved service. Certainly I hardly think this service will come up to the expectations of the people of the West India Islands. The minister will remember that when the Royal Commission visited the West Indies, evidence was heard at a great many points concerning the character of the steamship service then in operation. The complaints were numerous, and, I admit, in some respects perhaps it was justified, although not wholly so. The demands of the West Indies may have been rather exorbitant so far as the character of the service they demanded was concerned, but I submit that the service now afforded falls far short of the demands they made to the Royal Commission at that time. So far as the speed of the boats is concerned, the present service is apparently no improvement over the old one.
Oh, yes.

Under the contract with Pickford and Black the boats were to make an average speed of ten knots; the average speed required under the present contract is but eleven knots-the difference is very slight. Besides, the present service is to be a fortnightly one; I think under the last contract there were sailings from Halifax and St. John every twelve days, so in that respect the present service is not as favourable as the old. On the whole, I do not think that the Department of Trade and Commerce has given to this country the service to the West India Islands that was promised by the minister a year ago.

It certainly is not up to the expectations of the people of the West India Islands, and I think there is ample justification for the opinion which exists in the Maritime provinces: that the service is not sufficiently superior to the old one to justify increasing the subsidy from $90,000 to $340,000.

The West India service, from the time of its inception a good many years ago, has been a very difficult service. Any one who understands the West India Islands and their physical distribution, their peculiarities, so to speak, as regards ports, lighterage and other different requirements, will understand why it has been and always will be a somewhat difficult matter to please everybody, in the West Indies as well as in Canada, by any service carried on between the two countries. II may be that some people in the West Indies, taking what they would like to have as the measure, put up their anticipations very high, but I am led to believe that the sentiment of the West India Islands at the present time is fairly well satisfied with the boats that have been put on. One of the greatest complaints in the olden times was lack of uniformity and regularity and lack of cargo space. The opinion, I think, of the best men in the different islands is that we want in the first place is ships of sufficient cargo capacity. The Pickford and Black steamers did not have sufficient capacity, and great dissatisfaction was caused in that respect, not only here but in the West Indies. There is a perfect unanimity of opinion that the new service is entirely satisfactory in this respect. I have had communication with the principal men of the different islands since the boats have gone into service, and that is the information which I have, and which I believe to be a fairly true representation of the case. It is also essential that there shall be at least good accommodation for passengers, and that the first-class passenger accommodation shall be in the right part of the ship. That was not the case in the old service. The passenger accommodation in these boats is excellent accommodation. The first-class passenger accommodation is amidship, everything is modern, and is put on in a style and with a quality which makes a man who is travelling feel that he is comfortable and induces him to recommend the service to his friends. That was not the case in reference to the old service. I do not want to run down or criticise
unduly, but oftentimes old services are not as good as new.
That would be determined largely by the age of the ships I suppose?

The ship and the service have a kinship. If you do not have passenger accommodation in the proper part of the vessel where people are comfortable you do not generally have the service to the people themselves as good as it would otherwise be. I do not want to bring up old experiences, but I think that is a generally, fair statement of the case, so that as regards passenger* accommodation, unless the idea is for high tourist purposes, and with the idea of extending hotel accommodation and giving to the Islands a service which will participate in the entertaining and housing of passengers and tourists in the West Indies, as well as their carriage from port to port,
I believe you have a service in these boats which fills the reasonable expectations of the people of the West Indies. That is at least the impression that comes to me from what I have heard. I do not think that any service can be carried on satisfactorily with the West India Islands which would be what you might call a broker's service; chartering vessels and being dependent on charters was the great difficulty in the old service. Something would happen and then the whole sea would be scurried oyer to get a vessel which could take the 10 p.m. place of a vessel disabled. I think you get very far towards the solution of a good service when you get it in the hands of a steamship company which has one of the widest services in the world, and which has a fleet of vessels so large and of such different adaptabilities that the company can secure what they want for almost any kind of service. It has been that largeness of the company and the largeness of its service which has made it possible to put on four vessels which fill the requirements of the West India Islands, which, as my hon. friend knows, are peculiar; and which at the same time fill all reasonable requirements as to passengers and fully meet everything that is required with reference to freight accommodation. We get some other advantages. We have a powerful steamship company which is running its vessels in our service, but which also has lines of its own, and steamship companies with which it is in affilia-

tion which ran to other West India Islands and which skirt the 'Coasts of South America. One of the terms of the contract is that they shall make through rate arrangements so that a shipper from Ontario who wishes to send to ports in South America either on the west or east coast or on the north of South America, can send these goods on through bill of lading to the port of consignment. I think it a very great advantage and, as we have no steamship service to the ports in South America and yet there are possibilities of working up a good trade with South America, this will, to a large extent in its carrying out, obviate the necessity for a special subsidy for steamers to South America and will enable our producers and exporters to send to South America markets. I have not a list of the ports into which Canadian exporters will be able to have direct communication but it is a large and important series of ports. That we did not have with the other service and it is something to get a company of that kind interested in the Canadian service.
Does your control of rates extend to these different services?

The control of rates extends to the services which are laid down in the contract, and then the arrangements which are made for through rates have to be made as they can be made, but it gives the through line of passage. There is another thing; this company knows the West Indies better than any other shipping company in the world. It has had a service there for a great many years. It has an inter-insular service at the present time and at Trinidad and at one other port we get chances for inter-communication between the islands which are served directly under this contract and the islands of the West Indies that are served by the inter-insular line that is run by the same company. It is a fortunate thing I think that we have been able to make a trial under our new conditions with a company of the character, the financial strength and backing, and actual experience of trade in that quarter of the world, possessed by the Royal Mail Packet Company. I have had letters from passengers who have taken the trip down on the new steamers, and I have nothing but commendation as to the service, the accommodation and general agreeableness of the passage owing to the qualities of the ship and its service.

A great deal
would depend upon the weather.

I do not know that any
ship can be really comfortable when there is a tremendous sea on. I know I have never found one, but there are degrees of comfort in bad weather, if you are not absolutely laid on your back by seasickness. I had an experience of that when I came from London recently. I am not here to speak on behalf of any steamship company, but I must say that the Alsatian on which I came out and which is the newest acquisition of our Canadian fleet, is the finest vessel I ever travelled on so far as real comfort, service and steadiness are concerned. I am quite willing to give that advertisement to the ship, not for the ship's sake,
. but for the sake of any persons here who may want a good passage either way across the ocean.

I am not criticising the character of the boats in the new service, as I am the fact that we are paying $340,000 for this service, whereas formerly we were paying only $80,000 or $90,000, and the boats now in the service are not so very much better than the boats employed in the old service. I doubt if the improvement is sufficiently marked to justify the disparity in the amounts of the subsidy paid to-day and that paid under the old contract. I quite agree with my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that there is an admitted improvement in the general character of the ships as to their freight capacity and passenger accommodation. I think it is to be regretted, however, that the speed of these boats under the contract is not to be greater than eleven knots. I think it is also to be regretted that it is only a fourteen day service. I was in hopes that we would at least have a twelve day service from St. John and Halifax. I think there was under the old contract.

With reference to that, I have been told by people who ought to know, in fact I had the' information from the Islands themselves,-that a fortnightly service fits in with their wants better than a 12-day service, because it enables them to make connections which they could not otherwise make. I quite admit that this is a large subsidy but something had to be done.

The minister
must also admit that when he was soliciting tenders in 1912 he was anticipating a service very much better than the present one, not only in reference to passenger accommodation but to cargo

capacity, as well, and I think that had a deterring effect upon possible steamship contractors. My hon. friend has changed his mind very much indeed since twelve months ago respecting the service, that was actually needed for the West Indies. I must say that I am inclined to agree with what he has done rather than with what he thought should be done a year ago. Had it been known a year ago that the department would have been satisfied with a service of the character we are now having, possibly more favourable tenders might have then been received.

I am not sure of that. It is pretty difficult to say what would have happened, but I agree with my hon. friend in this respect, that there were thoughts then of a better speed. The passenger accommodation on these boats is pretty nearly as good as we were thinking at that time we might probably get. I could have got 15-knot boats and I could have got the extra passenger accommodation and flourish for what it was worth, but if I had, I should have had to pay certainly nothing less than half a million dollars. When you come up against a state of things like that, the disparity between these amounts tends to persuade you that you had better take the modified service and try it out for a time until you are a little more sure from actual experience than could be made certain by any amount of optimism or desire for such and such a thing. I believe that under the circumstances we have done about the best that could be done.

How is our
business going on with the West Indies?

Our business is increasing satisfactorily. There is this much about it, it has infused a new spirit in the West Indies in reference to Canada. There is no doubt about that. One indication of that is the very fine exhibit made at the Toronto Exhibition last year by the West India Islands, and the results that have come from that. The new service and the preference put together have made the people of the West Indies come to the conclusion that we are desirous of pushing our trade with them and they are now wishing to push their trade with us. I think that is worth a good deal, both to Canada and the West Indies, and counts as a very large factor in the development of trade. We have beyond all shadow of doubt an opportunity for a very largely increasing trade with the West Indies. Our competitor there for the products we send is the 61
United States, and our competitor has gotten ahead of us because of better passenger accommodation and especially because of better freight accommodation and more frequent sailings, but more especially in this one thing:	as I analyse it and come
down to the facts, what induces the smaller West India merchant-and it is a numerous class comparatively-to .favour New York, is that he can send to New York and get a small lot, say 50 or 25 barrels of flour, if he wants it, and have it sent down by the next boat. Under the old conditions, and to a certain extent yet, but it is being remedied, :he would send to St. John or to Halifax for a small lot with the idea that the goods were lying there and could be forwarded by the next boat, whereas the order had to be forwarded up to the producer in the middle of Ontario, if it were flour for instance, and there was all the delay and uncertainty of a long land route as well as a sea route, and consequently these small orders could not be filled with promptitude in a fair time.

Of course, the
steamship service has nothing to do with that.

that New York is a market tor Canadian flour outside of what is sent to the West Indies and in business arrangements they find it well to make connection with New York so as to secure both sides of the trade. But I think conditions are very favourable to our developing something of an interchange between the two countries.

What is the draught of the
steamers?
The table that I have here gives all the information except the draught, but practically the draught is light enough to enable them to do the work at the dock.
Bermuda would be the port with the lowest depth of water.

A difficulty is also encountered in getting in or out of the port of Georgetown, British Guiana, because of a bar which lies out. If your vessel is over a certain draught you will probably have to load at the docks and then go out beyond the bar and lighter the remaining part of your load into the vessel. That is the most difficult part of the West India Islands but these vessels are quite able to do the work at the dock.

Last year, when this matter was before the House, I called the attention of the acting minister at that time to the fact that these boats go up and down the bay of Fundy past the port of Yarmouth, and I asked him if it would not be possible, when you are making a contract with them, to have them stop at Yarmouth either one way or the other. Years ago a very large trade was done with the West Indies through brigs, schooners and the smaller class of vessels. A large quantity of fish was shipped from there. The port of Yarmouth distributes molasses and sugar to the western part of Nova Scotia and handles quite a large quantity of these . products. It would not detain the boats very long if there was water enough in Yarmouth harbour to permit of them coming in. The trade during the last two years has deteriorated very much indeed on account of not having vessels to carry it. A large quantity of molasses is imported into Yarmouth via Halifax and St. John for distribution in the western part of Nova Scotia, and a double freight is paid in getting the molasses there, whereas, if it could be imported directly at the port of Yarmouth by these boats which come from the West Indies a considerable stimulus would be given to this trad''. I would like

the minister to take the matter into consideration and endeavour to get these Royal Mail Steamship Company's steamers to stop at Yarmouth provided there is water enough in the port to enable them to come in. Boats drawing from nineteen to twenty feet of water can easily get into Yarmouth harbour now, and with that depth of water I imagine that these steamers could get there. I am sorry that the minister has not the draught of these boats. It is a wonder that he has not that information with him. What is the tonnage draught of these vessels.
My hon. friend credits me with being able to remember too much when he asks me to remember what is the draft of these vessels.
I did not ask the minister to remember; but he has a memorandum before him, and I supposed that he would find it there.

I have not that here, but 1 can give my hon. friend an answer to his question as to the tonnage and the passenger accommodation. The net tonnage of the Chignecto, the Cobequid, the Chaleurs and the Caraiquet would run from 2,975 to 2,999 tons, or in round figures 3,000 tons; gross tonnage, 4,746 to 4,889, the average being 4,798; capacity from 5,129 to 5,557. The first class passenger accommodation is 41, second-class 60 to 75, and third-class about 90. As to the port of Yarmouth, I would be quite willing to take the matter into consideration, but my hon. friend will see that after a contract is made, when we had some difficulty even as to the ports in the Maritime provinces which have been adopted, it is not an easy matter to make a change. If there is anything in the world which would tend to give me a sympathy with what my hon. friend suggests it is the predilection that the people of Yarmouth and nearby have for the good old-fashioned molasses of the West Indies. I remember the taste of the molasses from my boyhood days at this very minute, and I always respect the man who likes molasses.

I would imagine that perhaps those boats are a little too large, but I thought that from what the minister said about some of the ports of the West Indies they might possibly be able to get into the port of Yarmouth.

Are these
steamers provided with cold-storage?
Yes, and electric light and wireless.

What effect does the hon. minister anticipate that the placing of raw sugar upon the free list in the United States in 1916 will have upon the Canada-West India trade in that same product, whether much will be deflected towards the United States?

One cannot tell what the effect will be until the test has been made; but this will be a fact then as it is now, that the West Indies will have a preferential pdsition in this market whereas in the United States she competes with the whole world. As long as those conditions last, and particularly so long as there is sufficient market here for all of the West India products, which there is at present and will probably be for many years, I should not think that the effect would be very great.
Customs-salaries and contingent expenses of the several ports in the Dominion, including pay for overtime of officers, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $3,590,000.
How does the hon. minister account for the extraordinary increase r.f $300,000 in this item??

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Customs):
speechtext:
The vote last year was $3,290,000, and as stated by the hon. member it shows an increase of $300,000 for this year. Last year the total yearly salaries of officers employed at the various ports were $2,728,435. The contingent expenses of the ports for the year, based on the actual expenditure for the nine months ending December 31, 1913, were $394,745; the expenditure for overtime paid for the current year will amount to $134,000. Therefore the total amount of salaries, contingencies and for overtime paid will amount to $3,257,190. This will leave $32,810 that may yet be spent for increases up to the end of the fiscal year. This shows that the amount voted last year was practically all expended. We are asking for $300,000 for this year for the following purposes :
For salaries of additional officers including new ports and outports $150,000 ; for increases in salaries, $125,000; for increases in overtime paid, $10,000; for increases in contingent expenses, $15,000 ; total, $300,000.
The hon. member will understand that it is necessary to give an increase to officers throughout the Dominion, and there is also a demand for new offices. In the opinion of my officers and of myself, after going into the matter thoroughly, we do 61J
not think this is asking an unreasonable amount.	j

I am obliged to the hon. minister for the explanation which he has given; but I venture to suggest, with the utmost deference, that there are other expenses that go to account for this extraordinary increase of $300,000, that the hon. member has not given to this committee. For instance, at the last session of Parliament, I asked why Martin Johnston, preventive officer at Red Island in the county of Richmond, had been dismissed from office. The hon. minister told me that it was because there was nothing for him to do. I call the hon. minister's attention to the extraordinary circumstance that, having dismissed a man from office because there was nothing for him to do, he immediately appointed another person to do nothing in the same office. The dismissed official was in receipt of a salary of $100 a year for his services, whereas the information given me a few days ago by the hon. Minister of Customs is to the effect that Michael Edwin Gillies, the man appointed in Johnston's place to do nothing, was appointed at a salary of $250. That is a solitary instance; and I am quite sure, if the records of the department of the hon. minister were to be gone over, very many instances of a like nature would be discovered, which would go far to explain this increase of $300,000, in respect of which the hon. minister did not take us into his confidence a few moments ago.
If Martin Johnston, in the district of Red Island, was dismissed because there was nothing for him to do, I would like to know what justification the hon. minister had for immediately appointing a man to take his place. Of course, the man that the hon. minister appointed was the-brother of a defeated candidate in that part of the country, and I suppose he was entitled to some consideration from the hon. minister. How he can justify the increase of this man's salary from $100 to $250, when admittedly there was nothing for his predecessor in office to do, is something that I would like the hon. minister to explain.

If I remember rightly, the
place where Martin Johnston was stationed is in the same place at which Mr. Gillies is stationed. I think that Johnston was on one side of the river or bay and Mr. Gillies on the opposite side. Where Martin Johnston was, there was nothing to do; where Mr. Gillies is now there is something

to do, and for the salary that Mr. Johnston was getting one could not expect a man to do very much. My information is that Mr. Gillies is at Irish Cove in a different locality altogether, quite a distance away.
Only a few miles away.

Yes, but a few miles might make quite a difference. There was something to do at Irish Cove, whereas there was nothing to do where Mr. Johnston was employed. I really think it was absolutely necessary to have the station at a place like Irish Cove, where there was something to do.

The hon. minister is in no position to offer any explanation whatever. He says that Mr. Martin Johnston lived on one side of the bay and Mr. Gillies on the other. That is absolutely outside of the fact. Of course, I cannot hold the hon. minister responsible for any neglect of duty because he has not been able to inform himself as to the exact geography of the locality. I state to this committee, and the hon. minister of course is in no position to contradict me, that Johnston and Gillies live on the same side of the water. It is a farming community. Scarcely .any import business is done there. There is no vessel owned there. There is a wharf in the neighbourhood in which Mr. Johnston lives, and there is a wharf where Mr. Gillies lives. The same boat calls at both wharfs, and carries all the freight required in that community. Therefore, there is absolutely no foundation for the statement that more business is done at Irish Cove than at Red Island. I venture to say that the hon. minister has no information in his department that would justify him in making the appointment. I have no doubt that the minister received some such information possibly from Mr. Gillies, defeated Conservative candidate in my county, the brother of the gentleman who was .appointed to the office, but I venture to suggest that such information is not of a sufficiently reliable character to justify the minister in taking action upon it. This ' is a small matter, but it is nothing short of a public scandal that this man Johnston should have been dismissed from office	because	there was nothing	forhim to do and another man should have	been appointed to office	to	dothat '	nothing,'	and at a salary of	$250 ayear.	There is	no record, there is	no	information, in the department of the hon.

minister that would justify the minister in coming to this committee and stating that there is more work for a preventive officer at Irish Cove than at Red Island. As I stated, it is practically the .same neighbourhood; it lies along the southern shore of Bras d'Or lake, and the two places are a few miles apart, but as I said there is no more business to be done at Irish Cove than at Red Island. One steamer carries all the freight necessary for that community, and there is a wharf at each place to which the steamer comes; but, so far as business is concerned, if there was no business for Mr. Johnston to do, there is no business for Mr. Gillies to do at Irish Cove. But whilst the appointment of Mr. Johnston was made at the minimum of $100, the appointment of Mr. Gillies is made at $250.

Of course, the hon. gentleman knows the locality much better than I do, and I do not question what he says about it. But I have .stated that my officials informed me that where Mr. Johnston was located there was nothing to do; that where Mr. Gillies is located is some distance from the other and that there is something to do at that point. I am only giving the information which was given to me by my officials at the time.

I suppose the minister has
some record in his department of this information?

I discussed it with the Commissioner of Customs, Mr. McDougald, and he told me the position of the officers. There is no record; it was verbal.
Mr. KYTE. Did the commissioner make a report to the minister as to the necessity of -appointing a man at Irish Cove?

Certainly. I discussed it with -the commissioner, and he said that that was the place an officer should be, that there was more business to be -done at Irish Cove. That is the reason the appointment was made.

If the commissioner made
such a recommendation to the Minister of Customs, then I am bound to say he had not informed himself as to the facts. Surely there must be some record in the department on which the minister acted, if not from the commissioner then from some other source which was held to justify the minister in taking this action. I will ask the minister to look up the files, -and if there is any information in writing to bring it before the committee.
I do not think there is, but if there is, I shall be glad to bring it down.

What knowledge has the
Commissioner of Customs that the Minister ef Customs has not? The commissioner has lived here at Ottawa for many years, and I venture to say that he never visited that locality in his life.

The hon. member knows that we have inspectors travelling all over the Dominion, and these are in and out of Ottawa all the time. I suppose the commissioner discussed it with them. I do not know where he got the information, but I acted on his advice.
If the Inspector of Customs made a recommendation to the commissioner, that certainly would be in writing.
Not necessarily.

The Inspector of Customs is Mr. D. C. Macdonald, of Port Hood, who was appointed in May, 1911, and1 to my knowledge he has never been in Ottawa since. He has never met the Commissioner af Customs, and the commissioner has not been in Cape Breton. I am safe in assuming that any communication between the Inspector of Customs and the commissioner as to the appointment in Irish Cove must have been in writing and the minister can produce it.

The hon. gentleman misunderstood me. I did not refer to the inspector in the locality. We have inspectors travelling through the whole Dominion, officers attached to the main service, but knowing the locality well. It does not necessarily follow that the commissioner would have to get the information from the inspector of that particular district.
I suppose the travelling inspectors make report to the department?

They discuss these matters
verbally with the commissioner.

How could they discuss this matter verbally with the commissioner? The only travelling inspector in the Preventive Service was the late Captain J. W. Gordon, of North Sydney. He occupied the position up to a year ago. Whatever report he made to the commissioner, he made in writing. He would not leave his office in North Sydney to come here and recommend that a preventive officer should be appointed at Irish Cove. So, we get back to where we started: whatever recommendations was made to the minister to appoint a preventive officer at Irish Cove must be in writing; and if there is no recommendation in writing, there is none at all. It comes down, I suppose, to a recommendation from the defeated candidate in the county of Richmond to appoint his brother to that position after he had recommended the dismissal of Martin Johnston. Does the minister think he has made out a case for the appointment of Mr. M. E. Gillies to the office I refer to at a salary of $250 in view of his statement that Martin Johnston was dismissed because there was nothing to do?

I certainly think we were
justified in appointing a man at Irish Cove at a salary of $250.
Why does the minister think he was' justified in doing it? Has he any report recommending it to be done?

I stated to the hon. gentleman that the only information I have is from the Commissioner of Customs, who said 1 was justified in appointing a man at Irish Cove at a salary of $250, that there was more business doing there, and little if any doing where Mr. Johnston was located.

And so the
minister thinks he was justified in dismissing the other man?
We did not dismiss him, but let him go because there was nothing for him to do.

But this man lives
in the same place.
They are several miles apart.
How many?
I understand four or five miles.

If it were twentyfive or thirty miles it would matter little in the work of a preventive officer, because it quite infrequently happens that there is no work for a preventive officer in his own locality. In the Maritime provinces his territory usually extends over a certain portion of the coast line. If it be correct that the dismissed preventive officer resided at a distance of five miles from the residence of the newly appointed preventive officer, it appears to me that the explanation of the minister is hardly satisfactory; I think the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) is entitled to a better answer than he has received. The minister is in honour bound to restore the dismissed preventive officer to office and remove the

last one appointed. Surely it is evident that the reasons given are not sufficient for the dismissal of Mr. Johnston and the appointment of Mr. Gillies. I think the Minister of Customs might as well admit that frankly here and promise to restore the old preventive officer to his place. Cannot W6 get that promise?
I have explained to t/he hon. gentleman that we let Mr. Johnston go because there was nothing for him to do where he was stationed.
His successor is in the same place.
It is several miles distant.

A few miles makes
no difference.

It makes a great deal of difference where a man is located. The services of Mr. Gillies are more required where he is now than Mr. Johnston's were; there are more people living there, and there is greater possibility of smuggling taking place.	...

What work would
there: be for a preventive officer there?
The work of a preventive officer is to prevent smuggling along the coast.
Who would attempt to smuggle there?

I cannot answer that very
well.

How does the minister intend to distribute this increase of $300,000? Does he intend to increase the salaries of collectors of customs or preventive officers,

and does it apply to the inside or the outside service?

This vote is for the outside service; the law provides that officials in the inside service shall receive a certain annual increase. The practice during the last two years-and, in fact, the practice of my predecessors-has been that the officials of the department, the commissioner and the proper officers, submit a list of the officers from one end of the Dominion to the other to whom they think increases ought to be given, and as a rule their recommendations are adopted. These men know the officers and the conditions under which they work, and they are the ones who are the better able to recommend who should receive increases.
Has the minister the list of increases for this year, to which he has referred?
No. After the Estimates are voted, the Commissioner of Customs and his officials make up a statement showing the increases they recommend for the ensuing fiscal year.

On what principle do
they make these recommendations?

They simply add to the salary of each official the increase to which they think he is entitled for the ensuing year. Of course, they are sometimes unable to give them as much as they would like to, for the reason that vote is small; it is a small amount when you divide it up among so many officials.

Is there no principle
at all upon which such a list is made up?
Not such as there is in the inside service, where the law provides for an annual increase of $50 or $100.
The hon. minister has appointed a great number of new men to the customs service during the last eighteen months.

We had to appoint a good
many on account of the extra work.

I am told that a great
many of them have nothing to do.
I do not agree with the hon. member there.

How many has the
hon. minister appointed?

I think the total number of
new men is 768. Of course there are a
great many deaths, resignations and other changes which necessitate the appointment of new men. The opening up of new offices and the covering of new territory requires additional officers. Each year the work of the Customs Department is increasing. I was told by the commissioner the other day that between, I think. North Portal and Coutts, Alberta, there are 400 miles of territory in which we have no officer at all, and that an officer should be stationed every 25 miles for the convenience of incoming settlers and for the protection of the revenue. The same conditions exist, I think, in respect of the district territory between Emerson and North Portal. The commissioner and the inspectors have been urging that we should put a patrol from Emerson right through to British Columbia. Settlers crossing the boundary in these districts sometimes have to drive 50 miles to a customs office and then back again, which is a great hardship. In addition to that, there is a great pressure on the department for the opening of new offices all throughout the interior portions of the West, and it is difficult to give them the number they ask for. We are opening a new office in a place called Wainwright; between Saskatoon and Edmonton, a distance of 400 or 500 miles, we did not have an office at all. Even then the places are fifty miles apart. I think the hon. member fop Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) asked last year about a place called Edson. It is my intention to open an office in that locality.
Is not that office opened yet ?
It is intended to open one in that locality, and I think Edson is the only suitable place. The one at Athabaska Landing was opened nearly a year ago.

Edson is certainly the
only place; it would be a crime to put it anywhere else.
What is the meaning of the clause at the end of the item, ' notwithstanding any thing in the Civil Service Act.'

That is to permit of the payment of overtime to landing waiters. As a rule, they receive $850 a year. Their office hours are from eight in the morning until six at night, but of course they veTy often have to work until eleven or twelve o'clock, and they receive 30 cents an hour for this overtime. If we had not the

clause in, it would be impossible to pay them for overtime.

I called the attention of the minister to his appointment of two officials in Yarmouth at salaries of $1,000 a year, while we have three first-class officials, preventive officers Churchill, Potvin and Kirk, who receive only $850, besides their overtime. I trust the minister is considering their case, and will be prepared to give them an increase so as to put them on an equal footing with the two newly appointed men.
Churchill received $850 and $150 overtime; Potvin received $850 salary and about $100 overtime, and Kirk received $800 and $100 overtime.
But the other officials who are appointed at $1,000 get overtime as well. That is, Rogers and Boyd.
Rogers is not shown as receiving any overtime. Boyd had $23.40 overtime.

The three old officials are first-class officials, and it seems to me it was unfair for new men to come in and get more than they did after they had done their duty to the satisfaction of the public and of the department for years. I have nothing to say against the new appointees, and $1,000 is little enough.

I agree that the salaries of these preventive officers are very small. The usual salary in Ontario and the lower provinces is $850 a year, and then they have the overtime. The men who are appointed to work in the long room or to do clerical work, are appointed at a little higher salary, about $1,000, because they do not get overtime. I would be surprised if these men are doing the same work as the landing waiters and receiving practically the same overtime.

Boyd waits for the steamers the same as the others, and
11 p.m. earns a certain amount of overtime. When the daily boats arrive from Boston at six o'clock, they may have 600 passengers, and all the customs officials, except perhaps the collector, go down to the wharf to help pass the passengers. They earn their money.
Boyd received $23.40 for overtime. The overtime is divided among the landing waiters, unless for some reason one of the landing waiters cannot be present or an extra man is required.

Boyd attended the boats the same as the other three tide waiters. In fact, the clerk in the office and the three men cannot handle five hundred persons in the morning and get them off in an hour or an hour and a half, so that they can get the nine o'clock train from Yarmouth.

The yearly report made out by Smith Harding, the collector, shows Mr. Boyd to be employed in the long room. If they required an extra man he would be taken from the long room. If the hon. member will look over the list for the province, he will see that the salary of a landing waiter is about $850 or $900. I think myself they should get more, but if we increase their salaries by only $100 that would mean an increase altogether of $400,000.

How much has this
item increased .since the minister came into office?
The estimate that I first put through-it was prepared by my predecessor -was for $200,000 and $100,000 in the supplementary estimates.
How much was last year greater than the preceding year?

So that the increase
in this item since the hon. gentleman came into office is nearly $1,000,000.

That is not a fair way of
putting it. You cannot say that it is an increase. The salaries increase each year and they will continue to do so as long as imports increase, which makes more work.

I suppose .some customs officials have died, and that others have been appointed at -a less salary than was received by the deceased official? The only observation I have to make regarding this is that I think the cost of administering the Customs Department, particularly the outside service, is growing very rapidly. In the province of Nova Scotia alone-I have not the information before me but I know it is available-there have been unnecessary appointments to the customs service, and the payment of salaries to these unnecessary officials would probably aggregate $25,000 or $30,000. In a great many of the smaller ports of the province, appointments have been made which, I think, are purely political. I know of one person being appointed to the customs service in the county of Lunenburg at a salary

of $1,000 or $1,200 a year, and that official has nothing to do and will not have for a great number of years.
What is his name?

His name is Mr. Mack. I think the appointment is purely political. The appointment of Mr. Henley in the Preventive Service in the county of Halifax, was not, I think, a necessary appointment, and I have no doubt in many other places there have been appointments which were not absolutely necessary. I think the member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) will sustain me in that.

I cannot allow the remarks of the hon. gentleman to go unchallenged. I may say that the only customs official who perhaps was not giving value . for the salary he received, happened to be one of the fathers, I might say, of Liberalism in Cumberland county, and was appointed by the late Administration. At that time I think he was 65 years of age. He became incapacitated about a year ago, and was practically confined to his house, but rather than there should be any difficulty over the question he drew his salary until the day of his death a few weeks ago. That is the only case of money being expended where it was not properly earned, and surely hon. gentlemen opposite can find no fault in that case. There have been two appointments to the customs service last year in the town of Amherst, and I know as a matter of fact that they were necessitated in consequence of a report of an inspector of the Customs Department and not through any energy on my part. I had the privilege of recommending two men who were to occupy these positions, but the vacancies arose simply through the increase of business at that port. I do not know that the hon. junior member for Halifax can point his finger at any case and say that a certain appointment was a political appointment, or an unnecessary one. I have in mind the appointment made of a preventive officer at Spencer's Island in my county, and I venture to say that officer will collect little or no revenue, but ou the other hand his being appointed at that place will be the means of preventing a considerable amount of smuggling which has been going on there in years gone by, at least so rumour says. His appointment was due to the recommendation of Inspector Boak, who going down the shore saw that was a Strategical point where smuggling might take place. I have
no doubt the same condition applies to other places in the province of Nova Scotia. Let me say to my hon. friend that if he wants to point to Cumberland as an example of unnecessary appointments to the customs service, he is taking a very unfortunate case from his own viewpoint at all events.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, if I am not mistaken the question at issue between the hon. member for Richmond and the hon. Minister her for Richmond and the hon. Minister of Customs deals with the dismissal friends, who has, purely and simply, been replaced by one of our party. Hon gentlemen opposite have no reason to be shocked by what happens to-day, it being one of these trifling occurrences of every day political life. Let them go as far back as 1896, and they will find that greater grievances have already been suffered in this connection. To make the case clear let me recall that Mr. T. B. Cook was pensioned at the age of 46 and replaced by one Mr. Palmer, who was then 61. When the Opposition of the time asked for explanations from the Government, and wanted to know why Mr. Cook had been dismissed, they were told that he was too old; and he had, nevertheless, been replaced by a man who was his elder by fifteen years.
It seems to me that the case mentioned by the hon. member for Richmond is not as momentous as this one, and that he might have dispensed with reminding it.

I would like the minister to tell me, the next time we go into Supply, who has been appointed preventive officer at Arichat in the place of Lawrence Girrior, deceased?
